The I 12th Grand Master of Maso ns in California aml Hawaii. Donald Burns
McCaw, was born in San Francisco on April 20. 1928. the son of Dav id and
Enid Burns McCaw.
Hard work. long hours and thrift marked his teenage activity. He attended the
San Francisco public schools and continued his education at the University of
California in Berkeley. where he earned a Bachelor's Degree in Science with
a major in Bu s ine~s Admini stration. While he was at the University of California, he became a member of the Honorary Military Science Society of the Scabbard and Blade and, upon graduation in 1949. he was commissione d a Second
Lieutenant, Infantry Branch, Army of the United State ~.
Hi~ business career commenced with the nationally recognized insurance brokers. Cosgrove & Company. Our Grand Master determined to become a lawyer
and in 1954 ret urned to school at night while still employed full ti me in the
insurance brokerage business . He graduated from Law School in 1958 with a
degree of Doctor of Jurisprudenc e . In 1960 he became a founder of. and remains
an active partner in, the San Francisco law tim1 of McCaw & Barnum . He is
a member of the State Bar of California and for the pa~t e ight years has served
on the Ethics Committee of the San Francisco Bar .
On March 25, 1950. he married the former Camilla Burbank , who is known
to her friends as "Skip. " His son, Daniel Burns M cCaw. was born shortly after

FREDERIC E. CLARK

By Burton Meyer, Jr.
Frederic Edwin Clark was born in Norwich. Connecticut on June 28. 1889
and his many varied talents exemplified the talents of fabulous anll world renowned figures, the Connecticut Yankee.
.
Before coming to California in 1920, he marriell Louise Millard and they ~1:ed
in Hollywood for most of their married life . One of his hobbies was ra1smg
cymbidiums and he hall over one hundrell different varieti~s.
Freddie was engaged in the manufacture of steel tools tor 40 years anll operated his own business.
He was an Episcopalian and his service to God was manifestell in his daily
life and in his relations with his fellowmen.
Fred became a Master Mason in Wilshire-Garfielll Lollge No. 445 in May of
1928 and served as Master of that Lodge in 1935.
He joined the Los Angeles Scottish Rite in 1945 and served as Master of
Kadosh in 1952- 1953 . He served for more than 30 years on the Personnel Committee and was Chairman for many of those years .
He proved his acting talents in the degree work and was still doing so at the
time of his passing.
. .
In 1963 he was e lected to receive the 33° and was coroneted m December of
that year.
.
Appointed as an Inspector in 1944, he served with distinction for 27 years m
that important office of the Grand Lodge of California .
These are merely biographical sketches of the man and the Mason.
.
But what is the meas ure of one man? Some will say that it is the depth of his
intellect and his capacity for human understanlling and compassion. ~ome meas ure a man by the content of his commitment to o thers and by his sense of
justice. Others will say that it is his ability to lead other men and influence them
to believe in the rightness of the cause he espouses .
All of these, a nd more, are the measure of Frederic Edwin Clark , a Master
Mason's Master Mason.
If he could speak I know he'd say.
"Weep not for me, my friends, I pray:
It's just farewell and not good-by
For naught can break our mystic tie.
If Death were but the bitter end
And all our efforts just pretend,
Then we'd have nothing more lO gain
We'd all have Jived and died in vain.
The symbol of the Evergreen
Which we as Masons all have seen.
Gives proof that Life can never end
So travel on, our Faithful Frienll."

CHARL ES H . SEDAM

By John F . Robert s, Jr.
Bo rn in very humble s urro undings. one of five ch ildren of a sharecropper in
the little town of Edjington, Illinois, "Chuck" Sedam worked up to be a great
builder, a builder not o nly of struct ures, bu t a builder of men. As Pacific Gas
& Electric Company's Vice President- General Construction, he had charge of
a ll construction by the great utility from the smallest shed to a billion dollar
nuclear plant.
He was tough enough to deal with construction crews and their unions but
tender enough to show sincere affection to his lovely wife, Leilani and each of
his three charming daughters.
He took great pride in trainin g men in his crews who would seek his guidance.
Even when it was necessary to allmonish anll correct, he was always fair and
gained the respect of his workers.
He worked hard all of his life to overcome difficulties in achieving h is many
accomplishments. He learned earl y in life to be wary of any easily gained rewards when he discovered that one who paid hi s way to camp and offered g ifts
had ulterior motives in mind.
He worked his way through the University o f Washington , graduating as an
Electrical Engineer.
"Chuck" Sedam was a man of high moral s and principles, devoted to his
mother and family, and though strict with his daughters. compassionate and fair
with them. Each is happily married and have blessed Leilani and him with seven
granllchild ren. When each daughter was married, he gave her a shiny new dime
and said, "Always keep this, and if you ever need me use it to call me collect
and I' II come to you."
His work as a member of tbe Masonic Homes Board has been invaluable in
guilling the construction work of its present huge rehabilitation anll buillling
program, res ulting in the fo ll owi ng reso luti on:
WHEREAS, Worshipful Brother Charles H . Sedam, a Past Master of Loren zo
Lodge Number 709, was sulldenl y taken from his labors as a resu lt of an a ircraft
accillent on June 4, 1978: and

WHEREAS , The record of service of Worshipful Brother Sedam as a Trustee
of the Masonic Homes of California gives sufficient testimony that he was a
diligent and faithful servant to humanity in general, and to Freemasonry in particular: and
WHEREAS , He was a prime mover in the noble cause of Brotherly Love,
Relief and Truth; and
WHEREAS , His service to the Masonic Homes of California as the Chairman
of the Rehabilitation and Construction Committee fo r our Home for the Adults
at Union City and to his beloved Masonic Fraternity was limited only ~y the
uncertain tenure of life in its earthly form; and
WHEREAS, The Board of Trustees of the Masonic Homes of California , in
recognition of his great works as a man. and his treasured companions hip as a
friend. are desirous of furnishing physical evidence as tribute to his memory.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED. That the Board of Trustees of the
Masonic Hornes of California, by the power with wbich it is vested, and with
the concurrence of the Most Worshipful Donald B . McCaw. Grand Master of
Maso ns in California and Hawaii, does hereby designate the new Central Services Building of the Masonic Home at Union City as, "The Charle~ H . Sedam
Center"; and

GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE

All of us fell prey to the cold and dastardly villains who hid behind their white
hoods of hate, as they secreted their identities in the mechanism of printing,
foldi ng and mailing machines. The hearts of the perpetrators and the ir understand ing of Brotherhood can be equated to th e intellect of the cold and in nate
equipment they useJ .
Whether those who authored anJ distributed the hateful letter are ultimatel y
iden tified or whether their wretched selves remain concealed just as the notorious
" Hillside Strangler" or the "Zodiac Killer," they will have to li ve with their
own consciences and suffe r accord ingly.
I shall forever be grateful to the vast majority of o ur Jewish Brethren who,
through great effort, (and in many cases, perso nal sacrifice) exened a calming
influence among those who interpreted the writing to be anti-Semitic in nature.
rather than a vicious campaign tactic. as was believeJ by many. The task wa s
most difficult, for several of the concerend Brethren sought remedies through
outside age ncies an<l made demands upon your Grand Master , which , if implemented would have been as un -Masonic as the initial wrong.
Free~asonry shall long endure o ur eanhly shortcomings; yet. a lesson must
be learned from this painful experience . We must acquire the wisdom of conduct
and spirit of humanity so essentially necessary to attain the highest dream of the
prophets- that of a time when all men shall be Brothers.

My Brethren:
Section 1052 of the California Masonic Co<le mandates that: .. h shall be the
duty of the Grand Master to present, at each Annual Communication. a written
message. therein setting forth all his official acts during the year, exhibiting the
general condition of Masonry within the Jurisdiction and recommending suc h
legislation as he may deem nece ssary or expedient for the welfare of the Craft .''
Our great country endured a ho rrendous chapter in its illustrious history a~ it
emerged from the dark days of the Vietnam war, violence on the college campuses, bombings of public buildings and utilities, kidnappings of prominent people and highjackings of aircraft, ships and even school buses! We were to ld (and
all too many in positions of influence believeJ ) that God was dead and that
traditions were irrelevent.
This nation rose from the near destruction of that decade as a phoenix from
the fire, to have our children return with a serio us purpose in mind to their stu<lies
on the campuses of our great colleges an<l uni versities; to have our citizenry
reunite with their churches and synogogues; and to have the flame of fraternal ism
rekindled so as to bum again with brilliance. as a Brotherhood of Man under
the Fatherhood of God.
This was the state of o ur Nation as we embarked upon the !28th year in the
glorious history of our Grand Lodge last October. The world was mainly at
peace. The cowardly terrorists had reduced their activities. The environment anJ
beuuty of our land became a majo r issue. Science and technology. including
medical accomplishments. reached heights never before dreamed of. In California. the power of controlling the Government returned to the people through
the orderly and lawful process of expressing their opinions at the polls. And.
of importance to Freemasonry throughout the world, our Ancient Craft looked
ahead with opt imism in a manner unparalleled in its recent history .
Masonry is a Way of Life' And. being a part of life itself, the Fraternity is
comprised of men from every co untry and every clime, with all the strengths
and stamina, as well as all the frai lities and weaknesses, fou nd in society as u
whole. Certain ly , it is our fervent purpose to accept only good men and, then .
through our teachings and assoc iations. endeavor to help them become better
men. Yet. when we look for and find that the condition of our country and of
our Craft is essentially healthy . we are not so naive as to believe that we are
totally void of defects, for such is not the case.
In looking at the world at large, we observe border wars in Africa; religious
struggles in Ireland; terrorism and kidnappings in Italy; and man challenging
man on a variety of fronts, as has been the case from time immemorial. Just as
the memorial sculpture topping the east end of the Cali fo rnia Street wull of thi s
magnificent Temple includes fourteen marble fig ures depicting a titanic tug of
war between the forces of good and evil, o ur beloved Fraternity has not been
exempt from man· s inhumanity toward his fellow man . Sh o nly before our 1977
Communication , we suffered at the hands of persons unknown whose sole purpose it was to bring harm to all of Freemasonry by, in the most cowardly manner.
writing and distributing an anonymous letter with anti-Semitic ovenones .

GEN ERAL CONDITION OF MASONRY WITHIN TH E J URISDICTION

As the penJ ulum of society returns from the outer limits of its perio<lic oscillation, it creates an atmosphere wherein we may practice our progressive
moral science. We have built our theme- " Masonry is a Way of Life" upon

.
This most envied Jurisdiction has available to it and constantly working for
it, outstanding talent in every field of endeavor. When you consider the ability.
and even genius, of the members of our Grand Lodge assigned to our forty-three
Committees and Boards, yo u will appreciate, as does this Grand Master. the
professional manner in which the business of the Grund Lodge of California is
adm inistered.
I will not en umerate the attributes of any panicular Brother serving in a specific capacity such as on the Insurance or Jurisprudence or Finance or. Youth
Ac tivities or G rand Lodge Week Activities Committees . o r other Committee o r
Board. for each Master. Warden and Past Master th us serving is carefully chosen, is highly recommended and possesses outstanding skills .
I will state, however , that the singular most difficu lt task of a Deputy Grand
Master, i.s the process of selection of the most qualified Brother to serve Califo rnia and Hawaii Masonry from a cadre of e minent ly skilled Masons ready.
able and eager to toil in the vineyards of Freemasonry. As a result, those occasional few who accept the honor of the office and leave undone the. labor so
necessary to insure the excellence of our endeavors. do not long remain.

Master in their respective Districts. deserve our utmost praise. These men are

LODG E DUES

Lead ership is the key to the Temp le! Wher e
finances are low, it is a matte r
of provi ng the need for incre ased incom e . Many
Lodg es have not adjusted their
dues in ten years or more .
Yet, consi der what has happe ned to the cost
of runni ng our home s, our busi·
nesse s, our Temp le and our Lodg es. In 1968,
the Whol esale Price Index on the
1967 basis of 100 stood at 102. I . In the same
month of this year, the index was
206.4 . There is no magic in these numbers.
It simpl y mean s that if your dues
were $20 in 1968, they should be $40.4 3 today
. In other word s, if $20 was
adequ ate for an active and healthy Lodg e ten
years ago, that same Lodg e needs
$40.4 3 today just to keep even . If you exam ine
our dues struct ure, you will see
that the average dues in 1968 were $18 .39.
In 1978 they were $23.2 1 - an increas e of 26.2% rather than the 102.2 % neede
d.

MEMBERSHIP

Considering the much discussed problem concerning the decline in our membership,_ let us quickly put this matter in proper perspective . A review of num bers, without an analysis of supporting data, could readily lead one to believe
that Masonry is " on the decline " in this and other jurisdictions. Many promin~n_t. and certainly well meaning Masons have become herah.ls of doom agonmng over this matter.
It is true that our number has decreased from 244,000 in 1965 to 206,000 as
of our la~est census . This loss of 38,000 members is, of course, significant. but
concern is greatly reduced when we investigate the circumstances causing the
loss.
World War I ended in 1918. At that time. our Jurisdiction had a membership
of 68,000. In the succeeding years ending with 1929, the year in which the stock
market suffered its well known crash, the Fraternity flourished and our roster
listed 142,422 Masons on July 31, 1931.
w_e must ~ealize th~t o ur fraternal order tends to fluctuate in some slightly
varymg relat1onsh1p with the times and mores of society as a whole. Therefore.
a~ our State ~nd_ N_ation suffered through the throes of a terrible financial depression, our Junsd1ct1o n lost a net of 16,000 Brothers. so that in' 1941. there were
125,800 Masons on our rolls.
During World War II and the years of comparative peace which followed, the
Amencan e~onomy gained its strength: fraternaJism returned to its distinguished
place in society; and notwiths tanding the Korean conflict and early days of Vietnam, our ce nsus skyrocketed to a pinnacle of 244,586 in 1965 .
It is important to our careful analysis that we realize that the young men who
swelled our ranks during the period after Wo rld War I and until the time the
Depressio n struck, were only in their fifties and sixties in 1965, when our membership re~ched its peak. During the lo ng years of the Vietnam conflict , those
fift~ and sixty year o ld members entered their seventies. eighties and even nineties an~ tens of thou_sands of our beloved Brothers who joined our Craft during
the 1920 s went to their Celestial Home with the Great Architect of the Universe.
Thus, w_e readily account for the statistics by rational analysis and view the
declme in membership in perspective .

PROGRESS IN FIFTEEN YEARS

In his first message to the Craft, Past Grand Master Ira W. Coburn said
.. Freemasonry may be likened to a reposing titan - a large body having a great
potential but not- making full use of its inherent power .. . " He then established
a Special Commission which prepared a questionnaire to be answereu by the
Master of each Lodge and a more general questionnaire was prepared anu distributed to ten selected persons in each Lodge.
The huge mass of material compiled and tabulated was summarizeu in a tremendously val uable uocumcnt published as the "Repon of Special Commi~sion
on Masonic Practices 1963". In an effort not to lose sight of that important work
and further to use a thoughtful standard as a basis for my evaluation of the state
of the Craft. let us look at our Fraternal Jurisdiction in 1978 in relation to the
Special Commission findings of fifteen years ago in 1963.
NEED FOR BETTER LEADERSHlP

Leadership is the key to the Temple! Although generalization is not always
valiu, it is axiomatic that successful, healthy LoLlges have dynamic capable leaders . Those Lodges not blessed with such talented Brothers at the helm, flounuer
in a sea wh ich contains all the precious jewels of Freemasonry. but leaves them
unu iscovereu and unused .
As in 1963, no legislative action is required to overcome the uisability of lack
of leadership. The remedy is withi n the power of the Lodge itself to seek out
and train Brothers now possessing, o r having the potential to acquire, energy.
dedication. active imagination and administrative abilities.

28

PROCEED INGS OF THE

These essentials of leadership are not of necessity found in a Brother casually
selected or appointed because he is a personal friend of 1he incoming Master or
a hale and hearty fellow well met. Each Lodge should insist upon enforcing a
rule which is honored in the breach • a rule of single year tenure in appointiv e
Offices at least up to the Office of Junior Deacon . No Steward or Marshal should
be led to believe !hat he is part of a progressiv e line. Each should be instructed
and tested and evaluated each year. and those possessin g the greatest talents
should go directly to higher offices.
This procedure , if clearly establishe d and understoo d in a Lodge, allows many
members to occupy junior offices on a temporary or experime ntal basis. It qualifies greater numbers in our ritual. and it enhances a more intelligen t selection
of the Officers to occupy positions in the elective line.
lnier-rela ted with the foregoing . is the lack of willingne ss of men successfu l
in business and in communi ty activities to devote the number of years of service
most of our Lodges require of their progressi ve line. A capable man who can
"see the light at !he end of the tunnel" will be willing to devote his greaiest
energies. If the premise is valid that only three years apprentic eship need be
required to assume the office of Grand Master. no one should quarrel with requiring four years training prior to assuming the office of Worshipf ul Master.
To ask a highly capable man to devote five to ten nights 10 Mao:onry each
month for eight or nine years is, in my opinion, without valid reaso n and is a
major cause of lack of Lodge leadership . I urge you to commenc e your progressive lines with the office of Junior Deacon and to make thi s fact well known
in your Lodges.
Furtherm ore, either by tradilion or default. many of our Lodges require far
too much of our progressi ve line Officers' time. Often, we have our Officers
chair committe es for social and other activities which could just as well, or bet·
ter, be supervise d by others who will then have an opportuni ty to participat e in
a meaningf ul manner. We expect our Masters to serve on Temple Boards, to
appear at concorda nt and prerequis ite bodies, to attend youth functio ns and to
make other visitation s. when these tasks could be alternated among junior ofcers or others.
A tremendo us portion of the time of our Masters is devoted to ritual and the
constant work required of excellenc e in the same. It is my view (and the experience of successfu l Lodges) that a Master should be required to conduct a
Stated Meeting only in addition to his work in the Master Mason ·s Degree and
the Funeral Service . He should virtually be relieved from ritualis tic duties at the
beginning of the year rather than at the end. so that he may devote his time and
talent to administr ative duties.
Likewise . a large number of our Inspector s, in seeking to maintain the ex cellence of California ritual , tend to overlook (or at least relegate to a secondary
status) the greater importanc e of administr ative skills. I do not by this message
intend. in any manner. to lower our ritualistic standard . I do, however. seek to
place it in its proper perspecti ve. Much of an Inspector 's time is spent teaching
eight Brothers in each Lodge rituali stic skills. More responsib ility for this important function should be delegated to Officers ' coaches and a greater proportion of an Inspector 's time s hould be devoted to leadership or administr ative
training. Such realignme nt of priorities with necessary amendme nts to the

Inspector 's Manual. would be of tremendo us benefit to the Lodge when viewed
as an entity and would cause the loss of little. if anything, as far as the Candidat e

To summariz e my position quite frankly. I deem it far more important for our

CORNERSTONE CEREMONIES

The Grand Lodge, at the request of Masonic and public officials. conducted
28 Cornerstone and Dedication Ceremonies for Masonic Temples and public
buildings this year. A major event was held in Sacramento on May 15th, when
we were requested to re-lay symbolically the Cornerstone of the California State
Capitol. This ceremon y was performed in ancient form before the Governor and
many members of the Execu tive, Legi slative and Judi c ial branches of
Government.
The Capitol Cornerstone laying Ceremony and evening banquet. the latter of
which was attended by the Chief Ju stice of the Stale of California and chaired
by Chief Judge and Brother Thomas J. Mac Bride of the Eastern District of California for the Ninth Circuit of the Federal District Courts, was under the most
able direction of Worshipful Raymond Allen Young , Inspector of the 217th
Masonic District, with great assistan ce by Worshipful Frank J. Stimson, President of the Sac ramento Area Masters and Wardens Associat ion. This historic
day in the glorious annals of California Freemason!)' is reco rded in every essential detail by appendix to the Report of the Grand Secretary . Movies. photographs. tapes and memorabilia of every description commemorating the Ceremony and banquet are on display in the Grand Lodge M useum.
Cornerstone Laying Ceremonies have greatly enhanced the image of Freemasonry in the eyes of the public . The Ceremony is one of tradit io n and great
dignity and highl y i mpressive to all who view it. Every Mason should be alert
to the construction of new public buildings. and officials should be apprised of
our willingness 10 perfonn the An cient Ceremony.
A new movie of an actual Cornerstone Laying Program . produced under the
direction o f our Film and Creative Projects Committee. is available in our Film
Lending Library. It will serve the dual purpose of allowing officials interested
in having the Ceremony performed to view an actual event and it will further
be used as a training film to assist Masons in the various geographical areas of
our Jurisdictio n 10 prepare for such a Ceremony. The demand has been so great
that it may no longer be possible for the Grand Master and Grand Lodge Officers
personally 10 be present to conduct all suc h Ceremonies. By direction of the
Grand Master. however. they may be cond ucted b) others. and the film should
be of immeasureablc assistance.

Number 2. Certificate for Expelled Mason, Resto red .
Section 3514 of the California Masonic Code provides, under specified ci rcumstan ces, fo r the restoration of an ex pelled M ason by action of the Grand
Lodge at an Annual Communication. Such reslored Mason may petition for affiliation in a Lodge other than the Lodge which expelled him , but no provision
has been set fort h in the law for documentation o f his restored status so th at he
may visi t other Lodges.
Therefore, I recommend that Annotation "e" be added to C.M .C. Section
35 14 as fo llows:
" 3514e. A Mason restored under the provisions of the above section will be
issued a Certificate of Memhership by the Graml Secretary. advising all co ncerned of hi s status as an unaffiliated Mason in good standing. If the restored
Mason fails to become a member of some Lodge within the period of one
year from the date of the Grand Secretary 's Certifkate, he shall not thereafter
be en titled to any of the rights, pri vileges o r benefib of Masonry. except the
right to apply for affiliation."

Number 5.
Over the years of experience of thb Grand Master in dealing with the lav. of
this Jurisdiction, I have had considerable debate and discussions with many
learned Masons as to the precedent to be relied upon by Masters and oth ers
seeking to undertake their Masonic activities within the law of this
Jurisdiction .
I have maintained the very simple position that if it is not contained within
the California Masonic Code, it is not the law_ Yet, some Brothers have co ntended that matters reponed in Proceedings suc h as Committee Repo ns which
are approved by Grand Lodge but which arc not added to the California Masonic
Code as Annotations, are nevertheless law.
I strongly oppose this position for at least the following reasons:
A . Our law should be contained in a single volume easily accessible to all
Masons in this Jurisdiction.
B . Carried to its logical conclusio n, if we mus t searc h prior Proceedings to
determine what was adopted in Committee Repons , one seeking to comply
with o ur law must have available to him a library containing Proceedings
for the number o f years this Grand Lodge has been in existence.
C. Recommenda tio ns adopted by approving Committee Re pons require a
majority vote only and s hould not be given equal legal dignity to Resolutions and Gra nd Masters' Decisions which are adopted only after o pportunity for disc ussion and debate and by a 5/6th vote .
I do submit that Committee Reports and other matters may, and should
be , used as guide lines for those who, by familiarity with our la w or
throug h research, may seek the m o ut; however, this burden should not be
imposed upon a Mason seeking. in good faith , to comply with our law.
nor should a M ason , who fails to find so me obscure previously approved
Committee Report , subject himself to M asonic charges for his uninte ntional violation thereof.
Therefore , it is my Decisio n No. 5 that the law of this Juri sdic tion shall be
contained o nly in the California Masonic Code , as amended fro m time to time

Number 7.
A J7 year old applicant fo r Degrees committed a burglary in a mid-western
state when he was a mino r of 19 or 20 year~ of age. Although there were some
e xtenu ating circumstance s , the crime has bee n admitted by th e applica nt and he
served some four and one-half years in a reformatory for its commissio n .
Approximate ly three mo nths following release fro m the reformatory, the ap-

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

plicant commenced his studies in a university and subsequently received his
Bachelor. Master and Doctor of Philosophy Degrees. Thereafter he was employed as a University Professor for five years and now holds an executive position in business .
These facts are included to demonstrate the apparent rehabilitation of the applicant and, at the same time. to specify the basis for his ineligibility to receive
the Degrees of Masonry .
Section 2604 of the C.M.C. states in relevant part of that a person who has
pleaded or has been found guilty of a felony or of a misdemeanor which is
morally wrong in itself, is not eligible for the Degrees of Masonry, unless for
the reason that he did not commit the offense, he has been pardoned or has had
the judgment vacated. (Emphasis added).
The applicant has admitted the crime and there can be no doubt that a burglary
is an offense morally wrong in itself, whether it be categorized as a felony or
a misdemeanor. Thus, the applicant is not eligible for Degrees under the exceptions stated in C. M .C. Section 2604.
Due to my conviction that this man has been rehabilitated from the crime
committed while he was a minor, I researched the decisions of previous Grand
Masters to see if precedent could be found for an exception in this case. Past
Grand Master Henry C. Clausen. in his Decision No . 36, carefully traced the
origin of the applicable law from the old Ross Digest Section 875 enacted in
1875 to its affirmance in 1951.
Since it is not pertinent for me to do so. I will not reaffirm the conclusions
reached by Most Worshipful Brother Clausen in this decision. I will, however.
state that my research discloses no precedent upon which to rule in favor of
receiving the application.
No matter what my personal feelings may be in this individual case, the law
is clear. and therefore, it is my Decision No. 7 that one who has served in excess
of four years in a reformatOI)' for the crime of burglary committed when he was
19 or 20 years of age. is ineligible to apply for the Degrees of Mason!)' , even
though rehabilitated.

Those Brothers may occupy the esteemed office of Past Grand Master or the
honorable stature of an Entered Apprentice Mason. However. whether he is assisting the Grand Master in reaching a decision of great significance to the Craft
or whether he is in a Cornerstone or funeral procession or doing any number of
tasks in carrying out his responsibilities as a Mason. he is a person of valuea Brother in the truest sense of the word.
And. in this context. I shall ever be grateful to all of Freemasonry and to all
of my Brethren and, in particular. to my Dad , Brother David McCaw, a Master
Mason of fifty-seven years when he was taken to abide with the Great Architect
of the Universe in March of this year. To "Skip'' and Dan, my great love and
appreciation for their contributions to Masonry as a Way of Life.

ACKNOWLEDGEMENTS
It is traditional and proper at this point in the message of a Grand Ma~ter to
acknow ledge the special efforts of particular Brethren who have contributed significantly to Freemason!) in general and to this Grand Lodge in particular. I fear
that I will receive low marks in perpetuating this tradition. for with very few
exeptions. during my term as Grand Master. every Past Grand Master. eve!)
elective and appointi ve Grand Lodge Officer (including the staff of the Grand
Secretary's office), the Committee and Board Chairmen. Presidents , members
and staffs. the Inspectors and Lodge Officers and members. each ably responded
to the call and perforn1ed their duties.
One need not occupy this most honored ofhce for more than a few days to
reali ze that a Grand Master is but a seedling in a forest of giants. His administratio n must be of high integrity and his decisions must be made with tern ·
perance. fortitude. prudence and in strict compliance with our law. Yet. the
success and failure of our beloved Fraternity is due solely to the efforts of those
tens of thousands of Brothers wearing the lambskin apron.

45

CONCLUSION
In bringing this Message to a close, I wish you to realize that when you elected
me to serve as your Grand Master. you bestowed upon me the greatest honor
that any man could expect to receive. It is truly a position of dignity and respect
beyond that of kings and princes and potentates or any governmental officers.
Such honor and distinction. quite properly carries with it the necessary burdens and responsibilities which I have sought to undertake with the guidance of
our Great Creator and the labors of my Brethren.
If together we have done our part here on earth to promote and to practice
the magnificent lessons our beloved Fraternity has provided for us and the world
at large, it is because we have joined as a Brotherhond of Man under the Fatherhood of God seeking the universal truths and applying the age-old wisdom of
Masonry as a Way of Life.
Such goal may only be attained through our combined efforts as Brothersa com:ept most vi~idly expressed by our Brother Rudyard Kipling:
"For this is the law of the jungle;
As old, as true as the sky;
The wolf that shall keep it shall prosper;
But the wolf that shall break it. must die;
As the creeper that girdles the tree trunk;
The law runneth forward and back:
for the strength of the pack is in the wolf:
And the strength of the wolf is in the pack."
Thank you-Mahalo- my Brethren . May God Bless you and your loved ones.

October 23The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
In Decision No. 7 lhe Grand Master has prorerly decic..led that under our present law one who was con victed and was confined in a refonnatory while he was
a minor is ineligible to apply for the degrees of Masonry. However. the Grand
Master has applied a measure of time served in the worc..ling of that Decision
which this Committee feels would be subject to misinterpretation in the future.
He has usec..I the phrase ··served in excess of four years ." This might imply thar
one who has served less than four years for the same offense would be el igiblc.
We believe this was not the intent of the Grand Master. aml the Committee on
Policy and General Purposes approves of Decision No. 7. hut recommends and
expresses the hope that no addition or annotation be made to the California
Masonic Code because of the Decision.
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
Your Committee on Jurisprudence to which was referrec..1 the Grand Master'~
Decision No. 7 reports as follows:
To state it briefly. this Decision is to the effect that a man who has committed
a burglary anc..I pleaded guilty thereto or been convicted of the crime is not eligible to apply for the Degrees of Masonry because this crime involves moral
turpitude which makes a man ineligible for Masonry under Section 2064 of the
California Masonic Code .
Your Committee believes rhat the Decision is correct .
The case of
~tates thar "moral turpitude" is
everything done contrary to justice. honesty. modesty or goo<l morals . Burglary
is certainly contrary to justice. honesty and good morals and therefore is morally
wrong.
This certainly shows that burglary involves moral turpituM anc..I is wrong in
i•~elf.

We move that the Deci~ion be approved and adopted.
Adopted.

PROCLAMATION

Masons have long added the illumination of their kindly acts to the
great Light that guides each of us through the aching years to the
final peace of our eternal home.
The loving generosity of Masons has taken the hand of the troubled
child and the needy brother and widow and led them all to the
warmth, security and dignity of the Masonic Homes at Covina and
Decoto. At this time a tremendous redevelopment program is in
progress at Decoto making it more comfortable and liveable for its

It is further apparent that the per capita tax has been too low for several years .
To sustain an adequate cash flow to pay fo r the operations of the Grand Lodge
structure it was necessary this year to sell certain secu rities which had hitherto
produced income fo r the account.
In the absence of a balanced budget fo r th e Grand Lodge account in 1978-79,
it will aga in be necessary to sell income producing securities to meet the expe nditures of the G rand Lodge . In plain simp le language. the Grand Lodge in

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

all of its functions is spending more money than the total Grand Lodge revenues.
Several options are available to meet the problem .
This Grand Lodge can continue to dispose of our assets to help provide necessary funds or we can increase the per capita tax. The California per capita tax.
that amount which e ach member is required to pay as part of his Lodge dues
toward the total operations and functions of the Grand Lodge. is among the
lowest of those jurisdictions having 200,000 or more members.

ever, there were losses in the sale of securities and unrealized losses in the value
of certain other securities. These amounted to more than one million dollars.
The assets of the Endowment Fund were $37,268,118.00 at June 30th , 1978.
Income from the Endowment Fund continued to pay approximately one half of
the cost of operating the two Homes.
These several major assets are required to care for the present and future care
committments for the residents of our Homes .
Your Grand Treasurer recommends that present reserves should be allowed
to appreciate until there are sufficient funds for structural replacement in the
event of a catastrophe not covered by insurance.
This concludes the Grand Treasurer's report on the financial matters pertaining
to the four constituencies of this Grand Lodge.
The Grand Treasurer's responsibilities include jurisdiction over the physical
properties belonging to the Grand Lodge . In this respect the Grand Treasurer
intervened in the issue of the four-fold increase of the Assessment of the Columbia Masonic Temple at Columbia, California. Discussions seeking reconsideration of this unreasonable increase were not accepted by the Assessor of Tuolumne County. Accordingly, the Grand Treasurer filed an appeal with the County
Board of Equalization who heard the matter on Monday , October 17th , 1977 at
10:00 AM in Sonora. California . The Grand Treasurer was present and represented the Grand Lodge on that occasion . These efforts resulted in a reduction
of approximately I/3 rd of the assessment. It is the considered judgment of your
Grand Treasurer that no tax of any kind should be levied. The Columbia Temple
is an historical site restored by the Masons of California at a cost of more than
$50,000.00 and has no commercial or appreciating value. Perhaps the Jarvis Act
will take care of the problem. If not the State Recreation and Parks Department
are agreeable to "i!. revision of our contract and thi s should put an end to the
Tuolumne County Assessors determination to tax us.
In a related assessment matter, the Grand Treasurer almost exploded when he
received a tax bill for Peter Lassen's grave : but calmed down long enough to
get off a request for reconsideration and to have several of our Brothers in Lassen
County talk to the Assessor. Peter Lassen, a great Mason, a pioneer Californian
and the founder of Lassen County can sleep well tonight knowing that his
Brother Masons cared enough to make sure there are no taxes due on his grave.
The Grand Treasurer acknowledges with sincere appreciation the outstanding
cooperation of the Most Worshipful Donald Burns McCaw , certainly one of our
great Grand Masters: also the Very Worshipful Verne Hendrix . our Grand Secretary , as well as Worshipful David Hambly . o ur Assistant Grand Treasurer , the
very efficient Accounting Department of our Grand Lodge and in particular to
you my Brethren of the Grand Lodge who have placed your confidence in me
during these past eight years.
For all of this. my Brethren, I am most grateful.

The Masonic Homes of California
Because of the generosity of California Masons past and present . .. and the
prudent management by the Board of Trustees of the Homes , the general fund
increased by $4,334.000 .00 for the year ending June 30, 1978 . During this current Masonic year $2.934,000.00 was expended from this sum for capital improvements leaving a balance of $1,400,000.00 for transfer to our reserves .
After a net loss of $158 , 188.00 from sale and re-evaluation of securities. and.
after transfer of the cost of improvements made in the current year, the General
Fund of the Masonic Homes increased by $I .400,000.00 to an all time high of
$27 ,840,000 .00.
The renewal and replacement effort at the Masonic Homes in Union City is
estimated to cost $15,000,000.00. At June 30, 1978 we had paid out
$4, 700,000 .00 or almost 1/3rd of that total. The balance needed to complete the
work is available in the General Fund of the Masonic Homes . Obviously. money
used to make these necessary improvements may no longer be available to earn
income for the operation of the Homes. Whenever possible all Masons in California should encourage substantial donations, grants or other giving so as to
promptly replace these funds.
It is not possible to exaggerate the importance of the work and the outstanding
accomplishments of Most Worshipful Edward H. Siems, Past Grand Master and
former Grand Secretary in the establishment and growth of the Pooled Income
and Charitable Trusts of our Masonic Homes . Because of Ed Siems· efforts, the
totals of these funds exceeded one quarter of a million do llars at June 30, 1978
and has almost tripled since that time.
All of these life income gift plans meet the Federal and State requirements
for deductability and eventually all income will go to the Masonic Homes . Potential benefits in these programs both to the participants and the Homes are
unlimited. All California Masons should become mo re aware of these truly outstanding deferred giving programs wherein everybody wins.
Inspectors , Masters and Secretaries are urged to inform the Brethren concerning these new financial arms and invite their inquiries to the Grand Secretary's office .

REPORT OF THE GRAND SECRETARY
To the Most Worshipful Grand lodge, F . & A . M . of California:
Submitted herewith is my first report to Grand Lodge as your Grand Secretary .
Following the retirement last year of our Senior Past Grand Master. Edward H.
Siems. as Grand Secretary you elected me as his successor. It has been a year
of much reward and great challenge. While I had been Brother Siems' assistant
and worked closely with the Grand Secretary for many years . there was a myriad
of detail. offic ially part of that office, for which the Grand Secretary himself is
responsible . However, the transition has been quiet and effective. The friendly
support and understanding of the Grand Lodge Officers and the office employees
have helped in smoothing out any rough spots occurring as the result of that
personnel change.
The Grand Secretary's duties, as prescribed by law. include not only Grand
Lodge activities, but he is the official Secretary for the Masonic Homes o f Cal·
ifornia. the California Masonic Memorial Temple. the California Masonic Retirement Plan. the Masonic Homes Endowment Board and the California Masonic Foundation. All financial records, vouchers. supporting papers and books
for each of the entities whose records are maintained in our office are on file in
the Grand Lodge office .
All monies received and credited to the several accounts and released to the
custody of the Grand Treasurer. as provided by law, have been recorded. and
audits of these entities are available for review in the Grand Treasurer's Report.
The Finance Committee of Grand Lodge and its Chairman have reviewed the
details and disbursements made by Grand Lodge during the year. nut only as
to its operation and budget. but also as to direction and planning of all financial
matters.

The Commi11ee on Jurisprudence:
!he Committee on Jurisprudence has reviewed the applications for dispensat10ns _acted upon by the Grand Master and his approval of Life Membership
Re~olut10ns and find that he has acted properl y in granting or denying dispensations and in approving Life Membership Resolutions, except in four instances.
The application of Glendale Lodge No. 544 to ballot for and confer degrees
upon an applicant without reference of his application to a committee of investigat~on failed to show that due not ice of the meeting at which the ballot on the
application was to be taken and the purpose thereof was duly noticed to each
of its members .
The application of Kaweah Lodge No . 665 to hold an election other than on
th~ day fixed. therefo~ failed to show that it was based upo n good cause, and also
fa.tied to certify t~at II had been approved by two-thirds of the members present
at a Stated Meeting, and also failed to set forth specifically the reason s for the
request .·
The applicatioia of Melrose Lodge No. 602 to hold an election other than on
the day fixed therefor failed to certify that it had been approved by two-thirds
of the members present at a Stated Meeting .
The application of Maccabee Lodge No. 823 to hold an election to fill a vacancy failed to certify that it had been approved by two-thirds of the members
present at a Stated Meeting.
The Committee once again calls to the attention of Lodge Secretaries that
many of the applications for dispensation to ho ld an e lection other than the stated
time failed to _cenify that the requesting Lodge had complied with the requirements of Section 2502 of the California Masonic Code, particularly the requirements that the necessary number, namely two-thirds of the members present , at
a Stated Meeting voted to request a dispensation and setting forth specifically
the reasons for the request.
The Committee observes that although Resolutio n (9) of the 1976 Proceedings
of the Grand Lodge amending Section 324. subparagraph e (now Section 2046)
!o provide for outdoor meetings was adopted, the amending language was not
included m the 1977 pocket supplement.
We reco mmend that, except for the four instances, the actions of the Grand
Master be approved, and that in the cases of Glendale Lodge No. 544 and Mel ·
rose Lodge 602, and Maccabee Lodge No. 823 the Lodge be requested to furnish
proper certification, and that in the case of Kaweah Lodge No . 665 the Lodge
be requested to furnish proper cenification and the reason s for its request.

same arc ratified. affirmed. and approved.

GOLDEN VETERANS AWARDS
TRIAL R ECORD No . 2 I 24

The accused was convicted in a California co urt o f murder in the second degree . At the trial by his Lodge, the accused presented testimony to ex plain his
acts. The T rial Commissio ners determined that lhe accused was guilty of the
crime of murder in the second degree, but not guilty of un -Masonic conduct.
These two results are irreconc ilable . One who is guilty of murder in the second
degree is necessarily g uilty of un-Masonic conduct. The contlict must be resolved in o rder that there be a valid result . and your Committee is unable to
determine in what manner the reso lution is to be made .
The Trial Review Committee is mindful .of the problems c reated for any Lodge
by reason of a Masonic T rial and parcicularly of a retr ial . The ca~c must be
retried in its entirety unless proceedings are resumed and all of 1he fo llowing
co nditions are met:
(I) Eac h and every one of the Trial Commissio ners who served at the trial

is willing and able to assemble as they did for tbei r de liberatio ns immediately after the trial, for lhe purpose of resolving the conflict: and
(2) E ach and every o ne of such Trial Commissio ners states on his honor as
a Master Mason that he (a) has a clear and acc urate recollec tio n of all of
the trial proceed ings and (b) has not, since the close of the trial, received
any facts, opinio ns, or othe r information which would in fluence him in
hi s present resolution of the conflicting results .

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Assistant Grand Lecturer- Assistant Grand Lect urer

" M ay they be patriots and statesmen who are wise in council. powerful in
debate and fearless in action. May sy mmetry and o rder rest upon each line and
curve of thi s magnificent structure; may s trength and beauty characterize each
arch and pillar; may the grandeur of its proportions attract the admiration and
gladden the heart of eve.ry lover of order and progress; and fro m its lofty dome,
may the glorious ensign of our country. with stars and stripes forever bright ,
wave proudly and triumphantly.
"Eac h of you here assembled on thi s historic day in Sacramento. should have
a keen sense of awareness of your role in history as we place the time capsule
(whi ch we call a casket) into the stone here befo re you.
" You sho uld know that the ceremony which you arc about to witness has
been transmitted essentially unimpaired throughout the ages, as is the case with
all Masonic teachings and traditions. This Cornerstone laying ceremony had its
origin in a great cathedral building era which lasted in Western Europe and Great
Britain from the twelfth through the sixteenth cen turies . During those four
hundred years, Masons (which is another te rm for builders) constructed those
magnificently beautiful Gochie Cathedrals- many of which still stand .
" The grace and symmetry of those edifices were totally dependent upon the
skill of the stonemasons in making a foundation stone or cornerstone which was
perfectly square, and set exactly level and plumb.
" It was e ssential that the first stone or corners to ne was exactly square, level
and plumb. for it was from that stone alone that every other s tone used in the
construction of the edifice was squared. leveled and plumbed .
" With modem science and technology, it is no longer necessary to construct
a building upon a cornerstone and therefore , the ceremony which we are about
to co mmence is s1mbolic and is to remind us that temperance. fortitude , prudence and justice m government together represents th e cornerstone and foundation of freedom.
..The working tools of a Mason which arc used in the Ceremony are likewise
intended symbolically to remind us of the great moral principles which form the
cornerstone for a way of life:
"The Square teaches us to square our actions; the Level denotes equality; the
Plumb admonishes us to walk straight and tall before God and Man; and the
Trowel is used symbolically to spread the ceme nt of Brotherly Love and
Affection.
"With th is hi storical background, we s hould contemplate o ur place here today. realizing that Maso ns have not o nl y laid the Cornerstones for hundreds of
public schools and other public buildings here in California (including the original C ornerstone for this Capitol of our State one hundred seventeen years ago
today on May 15. 1861 ); but we may also close o ur eyes and visualize the Father
of o ur Country. George Washington. while serv ing in the dual capacity of Worshipful Master o f Alexandria Lodge No. 22 of the Commonwealth of Virginia
and President of the United States of America in 1792, standing before an audience of citizens such as yourselves. performing thi s identical ceremony while
layi ng the Cornerstone for the Capitol of our Nation in Washington, D.C.
" In accordance with the leachings of our Institution. it is our duty, before
entering upon any great or important undertaking, to invoke the aid and blessing

The parade thus formed proceeded at I: 15 P.M. along "L" Street to 10th
Street and into the State Capitol Grounds where a platform had been erected for
the accommodation of the Grand Lodge Officers. the State Government Officials
and the members of the Legislature. The Grand Master. surrounded by the other
Grand Lodge Officers. was seated in the center facing the State Government
Officials and the members of the Legislature. Table.'> were set up next to the
rostrum and the cornerstone upon which were placed the Holy Writings. the
Book of Constilutions. the Golden Vessel of Com. lhe lwo Silver Vessels containing Wine and Oil. the three large Lights, the five Orders of Architecture and
the Working Tools.
The Ben Ali Shrine Temple Band entertained the assemblage with its music.
The Reverend Walter Link, the Assembly ·Chaplain. gave the Invocat ion. The

The Grand Orator rhen delfrered a portion of rhe eloquent 1861 orarion:

THE ADDRESS
Mr. Samuel M . Wilson . of San Francisco, said-

"Fellow citizens; today a great state lays here the cornerstone of her Capitol,
the First Capitol ever thus dedicated upon the Pac ific Coast. On the an nouncement of such a fact as this, many associations come clustering thick and fast
upon us; many recollections of the past , pleasant and sad, and many a far stretching thought of the anticipated and doubtful future . Upon a ll such occasions how
much the rich eloquence of such untold thought surpasses their attempted utterance? With solemn fonn and appropriate ceremonies, in the face of day. in the
presence of citizens, the military and the civic societies; before God, and the
three great branches of a constitutiona l Government, we dedicate here today a
temple significant at once of our progress and civilization, significant of our
wealth. strength , and self-reliance; significant of our bright anticipations of fu.
ture stability and greatness. Many a nation has built her mighty structures by the
driven labor of her wretched workmen , the enforced skill of her toiling artisans ,
and heavy exto rtions from her unwilling citize ns . Many a lofty column has lifted
up a gorgeous palace, built with the ill-gotten treasure wrung by a tyrant fro m
his oppressed subjects. And the famous Capitol of Rome - the great temple of
Jupiter Capitolanus was decorated with the rich spoils plundered from neighboring nations. But here the people themselves , through their own chosen representatives, have voluntarily undertaken this great work, and freely appropriated their own treasure for its construction. Its object is not ostentation and
display; it is not to commemorat e any past event; but it looks only to utility, to
the common good and general welfare . A spot has been selected, untrod by foot
of c ivilized man when the Ame rican Revolution began and warmed into existence a new nation of thirteen feeble colonies, and here we stand today representatives from all those o ld colonies and their younger sister States , a prominent
and respected member of that nation, even before all who mingled in that glorious revolution have taken their "chambers in the silent halls of death. "
"We have a land teeming with the richest ores that lay upon the surface and
yielded to the simplest implements of labor; and we have a soil susceptible of
the easiest culture, and yielding the most abundant harvest. But above a ll, our
forefathers had furnished us those pure principles of right government , in their
true co nstitutional form, ready fashioned to our hand. filling our demands. ministering to a ll ou r requirements , and enabling us, in the short circle of a few
months. not only to fo und and establish a new State, but to set all the complicated and delicate machinery of a practical government into full and successful
operation . From the workshop of their mighty brain, and from the forge of revolution, we received the well-shaped principles of constitutiona l liberty. We
have accepted them; we have appropriated them; and today we are enjoying the
rich fruits of their wise use and proper application . We stand , after the lapse of
but little over ten years, a great a nd prosperous State . We point with glowing
pride , to mines unequalled, to agricultural resources unsurpassed, to growing
manufacturin g, to an increasing commerce, to internal improvements, to general
intelligence and regard for the laws , to a rising and upward tendency in morals.

to numberless churches, sc hools and institutions devoted to the causes of religion , mental improvement , fraternity and benevolence . Like our own flowers
and fruits, we have grown, flourished and ripened, with a rapidity whic h makes
our story sound like an Arabian tale . To soil, to climate, and to fortunate circumstances , we owe much ; but I repeat, that above all we are indebted to our
glorious nation and Union. and to those mighty men who founded them .
"All over this vast country. from the great lakes of the Nonh to the reefs of
Florida, and the delta of the Mississippi, and from ocean to ocean. the great
principles, by our forefathers inaugurated on this continent, are the vital and
active principles of the Government. Under their influence, embodied in our
unequalled Constitution and Union . the dense forests have given place to the
waving fields of golden grain, and at the river' s side and o n the margin ef the
bay, have grown up great cities . teeming with active brains and ·industrious
hands . The solemn silence of the grand prairie is broken by the shrill whistle
of the car, as it rolls its ric h commerce and li ving freight from city to city . The
huge steamship plies her safe tract through regions only known of yore to the
sea-monster. From a thousand chimneys the smoke of a thousand arts. is see n .
and the humblest home shows the triumphs of the American anisan . The hum
that comes from the industrious city mingles with the hum of the country school
house; and the iron rods poi nting the spires of myriads of churches show th at
we know how not only to escape the lightning of the angry clouds, but also the
lightning of an angry God . Thousands of strong hands and honest hearts have
left the sac red precincts of their native lands to enjoy the better life th at awaits
them here. We have more than quadrupled our territorial possessions. with honor
and good faith to all. We have plumbed the depths and found out the courses
of Old Ocean· s currents and, wi th the magnetic spark , we have circled the continent and crosse~ the deep sea. We have penetrated the polar regions far beyond
all other nations, and our astronomers. wandering into the unknown regio ns of
the heavens, have di scovered new worlds . We have advanced to the front ranks
of the very first nations of the earth, and won for ourselves the admiration and
respect of the world. For what do you seek that America has not afforded ? Of
such a country , what could be said too much in praise? What could be said that
would be exaggeration ?
"All admit the tremendous difficulties and embarrassme nts that surround the
public affairs . I will not offend you by arrogating to myself the power to suggest
a solution . But there is still one voice that all listen to with attention. There is
one fountain of truth, purity and wisdom at which all may drink. There is one
name, next to Deity, most loved throughout the earth . It is that of Washington .
"There are four things which I humbly conceive are essential to the wellbeing, I may even venture to say to the very existence of the United States as
an independent power. First - An indissoluable union of the States under one
Federal head. Second-A sacred regard to the public justice. Third-The adoption of a proper peace establishmen t; and Fourth- The prevalence of that pacific
and friendly disposition among the people of the United States , which will induce them to forge t their local prejudices and policies; to make those mutual
concessio ns, which are requisite to the general prosperity; and in some instances
to sacrifice their individual advantages to the interest of the community . These
are the pillars on which the glorious fabric of our independency and nationa l

our Capitol, let us pr~pare for this trial, with that high purrose, that unswerving

far off future, millions of freemen shall throng this wiJe coast. and looking over
these broad stones. shall curiously inquire who and what were the founders, may
they learn of men who loved and followed the flag their fathers loved and followed; men who sought peace f()r the sake of the Union but who loved the Union
better than peace. And above all may they find that we had some share. little
though it may be , in restoring harmony and fraternity to our di st racted country,
and in handing down the succeeding generations that flag unsullied and that
Union unbroken .

The Trustees of the Masonic Hornes of California. a charitable corporation
organized under the laws of the state of California, present the eighty-sixth annual report on the Masonic Hornes of California for the fiscal year, July I. 1977,
through June 30. 1978 .

for the purpose of organization. The election of Donald B. Ingalls, Deputy Grand
Master. Vernon L. Gordon, Senior Grand Warden. and H. Douglas Lemons.
Junio r Grand Warden, was fonnally reported to the Board and on motion duly
made, seconded, and carried they were elected members of the Board. In addition to the Grand Lodge Officers, the Board was composed of the following

On June 4, 1978 , the Masonic Hornes Board of Trustees and California Freemasonry lost one of their most faithful and devoted member~ and brother!> with
the death of C harles H . Sedam in an airplane accident in Canada. ·'Chuck"'
Sedam was a Past Master of Lorenzo Lodge No. 709 and Vice-President of
General Construction, Pacific Gas and Electric Co. He had chaired the building
rehabilitation committee at Un ion City and had directed the construction and
general development since the program commenced. providing his accumu lated
knowledge, ski ll, and expertise to the project. He has been sorely missed and
the Trustees have dedicated the program of rehabilitation at the Masonic Home
to his memory.
Grand Master Donald B. McCaw appointed Ralph M. Hinds. Past Master of
Alamo Lodge No. 122. to serve the unexpired term of Brother Sedam . For 23
years Brother Hinds was the Inspector of the I 18th Masonic district.

ORGANIZATION OF STAFF

Overall direction of Masonic Ho rnes is unde r the capable supervision of Raymond H . Howe (346), a former Trustee and experienced business man ager. As
executive Director. Brother Howe carries out the policies of the Board of Trustees in the management of both Hornes.
J . Burton Brown (334) is displaying exceptional talent as Adm inistrator of the
Home at Union City. His leadership. skills, and empathy for the residents make
him eminently qualified for the demanding tasks of his assignment. He has the
support of a fine staff and of his wife Ruth in helping to make the Home o ne
of the finest in the United States .
James C. Bl aine (104) commences his thi rteenth year as Administrator of the
Home for Children at Covina. Bac ked by a well trained staff and the help of his
wife Dorothy, Brothe r Blaine provides th e kind care. love and protection the
Masons of California want for their ·'adopted" children.
Personal interviews with applicants. written reports to the Board, and contacts
with government agencies are but a few of the duties of the Homes representatives. Sue Collins provides such laison service in Northern California, while
Martha Quick, herself a graduate of the Covina Home. has for many years represented the Homes in Southern California. Martha has reti red after many years
of dedicated work for the Masonic Homes and the Board is grateful for her
devotion and the value of the services she ha!> rendered.
MEETINGS

During the years the Board held meetings monthly near the Los Angeles and
San Francisco airports, in addition to meetings at Union City and Covina, wllh
a long term planning meeting in Santa Barbara. In addition. committees on rehabilitation at U~ion City, scholarship grants. special projects, and budget and
finance met on other occasions during the year.
FINANCIAL
With assets approaching $75,000,000, an amount which includes the value
of the two Homes properties, the general fund and Endowment Fund investments
at cost, it is necessary and proper to apply the same ernnomic principles of
budget and control as in any private o r public business. Proposed budgets are
carefully scrutinized by the Board. As a resu lt . the Homes corporation continue~
to operate within its ava ilable income. despite the upward pressures of inflation
and the increase in the cost of living .
The extent of these forces is best demonstrated by comparing the cost of operating the Homes in 1958 with the cost in 1978 . In 1958 with _appr~xirnat~ly
the same population as today. the total costs of Homes operations including
administrative and general expenses was $857 ,000 . Jn the fiscal year 1978 comparable costs were $4,769,000. Over the twenty-year period the annual _rate of
increase has averaged eight and one-half (8 1h % ) percent. Due to the income
from the Endowment Fund and the gifts and bequests of a generous Fraternity
and the many friends of the Hornes. the annual income has kept pace . In 1958
revenues were $805,000. In 1978 the total income exceeded $5.000,000 .
The Endowment Board and Chairman Robert Hilts deserve the plaudits of the
Masons of California for their untiring efforts in increasing t he Endowment

Fund. Added to this effon has been the _work of Lodge Endowment Chairmen.
Masters, and Secretaries, all of whom have made the Endowment campaign a
year-around activity.
With the continuing growth of the Endowment Fund and the gift_s .mad~ by
donors during life and by wills. coupled with a business-oriented admm1strat1on.
there is no need to increase the per capita , and the Trustees recommend the
continuance of $1 .00 per member for the support of the Homes.
A complete financial statement of the Masonic Homes of California a~d of
the various funds including the Endowment Fund will be found in the published
proceedings. These statements deserve the review and study of every mem~er
of Grand Lodge since there is represented a full disclosure of the financial affairs
of the Homes.

POOLED INCOME FUND
When Past Grand Master Edward H. Siems announced his retirement as Grand
Secretary at the last Annual Communication , Masonic Homes became the beneficiary of this dec ision with his appointment as Director of Charitable Gifts for
the Homes . As a result of his efforts during the past year nearly $600,000 . have
been placed in the Pooled lncome Fund and other trusts . The funds pro~ide a
lifetime income for beneficiaries with the Masonic Homes being the ultimate
recipent of the funds.

UNION CITY OPERATION
The Home at Union City, known with affectio n for many years as the Decoto
Home, is the personification of the trust Masonry has had in brotherly Jove. It
is here that our older brethren, their wives, and wido ws reside with dignity and
companionship. It is here that every attempt is made by a devoted staff to provide
the residents with the comfons, the security, aml most of all the love they richly
·
deserve in the s un set years of life.
The average number of residents in the Home during the year was 330. Of
interest is the fact that the average age of the 42 guests admitted to Union City
during the past year was 90, while the average age of the residents who died,
45 in number, was 87.
At the last Annual Communication your Board of Trustees reponed extensively on the rehabilitation program then in progress at Union C ity involving the
expenditure of more that $ 12 million dollars. Now completed is the life safety
system, the upgrading of buildings to code requirements . the seismic study, the
renovating of the water supply system. the installation of a fire hydrant system
around the buildings, fire door and smoke detectors, and the demolition of the
building u~ed for dining and assembly and a dormitory building which had been
declared unsafe. In addition. new medical equipment and furnishings were provided for the sk illed nursing facility.
The north wing of the residential area has been remodeled to provide each of
the attractive new living quarters with a private bathroom , while the same work
in the south wing is presently in the finishing stage . By the middle of 1979 the
new Central Service Building will be nearing completion with dining and kitchen

123

COVINA OPERATIONS
The Home at Covina continues to provide the finest facility in the country
where children live together in family groups. growing up in an atmosphere of
affection, panicipating in the life-learning processes. and eventually graduating
from the Home into higher education and to adulthood.
The interest and concern for the Covina children does not cease as they graduate from high school and leave the Home. Com munications with the alumni
continue for years through letters and annual get-to get hers. Currently. eight
graduates are receiving a combined total of $21,000 annually in scholarships as
they continue their quest for funher knowledge in community colleges and
universities.
The primary philanthropic project for the International Order of Job 's Daughters in 1978 is a patio area complete with barbecue for the use of the children
and for visitors. Thoughtful gifts such as this and the bus the Job's Daughters
donated to the Home at Union City two years ago demo nstrate that we are truly
one Masonic family .
Detailed reports of the Administrators will be included in the proceedings of
thi s Annual Communication. Their readi ng is highly recommended.

SUMMARY
The Trustees are grateful to Grand Master Donald B. McCaw for the leadership and co unsel he has continued to provide to the Board. The Board gives
special thanks to Past Grand Master Edward H . Siems. His sixteen years as
Secretary to the Board continue to inure to the benefit of Masonic Homes and
his serving the Ho mes as Direc to r of Charitable Gifts has been and will continue
to be a valuable co ntribution.
Grand Treasurer Chester R. MacPhee has given the Board on-going financial
direction. and. with the assistance of Trustee Roben Mason. has expeditiously
sold properties donated to the Masonic Homes .
Grand Secretary Verne W . Hendrix and the offices of the Grand Lodge have
made a valuable contribution to Masonic Ho mes in furnishing accounting and
financial control services . The work of Irene Harrigan is especially appreciated.
Legal advice and counsel have been capable provided by Varnum Paul (169)
and the Trustees are grateful for hi s continuing interest in Masonic Homes.
The Trustees wish to extend their thank s to Raymond A. Howe , to J. Burton
Brown. to James C. Blaine and the staffs at Union City and Covina for their
loyalty and dedication. Finally. the Trustees place the highest value on the s upport and e ncouragement the Masons of California have given to the Masoni c
Homes without whose interest the Homes co uld not exist.

I. ACTIVITIES
Ac tivities mean different things for different people. Daily habits create "activities" for some , while special events or trips may be the only activities that
appeal to others.
As in any family, certain special events are traditions and some of ours continue on year after year. A trip to Monterey , the lee Follies, an Arts and Craft
Show, the Halloween Costume Party , and lunch at Fishermans' Wharf were
again well attended. We, also , greatly enjoy the traditional Monday Night Entertainment at Grand Lodge, Visitatio n Day, our Christmas Party and the Grand
Master's Reception, whereby, we are hono red with the presence of the Grand
Master and members of the Grand Lodge family. A new tradition has been incepted at the Ho me due to the celebration of the Bicentennial Anniversary in
July, 1976. We had our Second Annual County Fair on July I , 1977 and enjoyed
a " Roaring Twenties" theme with many res idents, friends and relatives joining
in the festivi ties. A very popular part of the fair was an o ld fashioned .. Dunk
Tank" where residents and e mployees made it a "wet day" for the administrato rs. A new activity, introduced in March. will hopefully continue and become
anoth er tradition. A. number of male resident s, all belonging to different Shrine
Clubs met to form a "Fez Club" and now meet once a month for lunch and a
program .
Ho nors bestowed upon residents we re highlight ed on May 3rd when Brother
John Blunck reached the century m ark in birthdays. He becomes the third member of this very s pecial part of our family ; 100 YEARS OR MORE. Scottish Rite and John McGraw (age 98) was ho nored with a 50-year pin from

recognizing 75 years as a membe r.
Four of our couples were acknowledged as they celebrate d more than fifty
years o f marriage. Mr. and Mrs . Carl Bechto ld have the honor of sharing the
mos t years together; 60 years on March 11th .

REPORT OF THE ADMINISTRATOR
MASONIC HOME, COVINA

Again. thanks to our ''Masonic Family" for making this past year a happy
one in the lives of the children in ou r care . Your love and support are appreciated
by our children, staff and Board of Trustees.

It is with pleasure that the annual report for the Masonic Home for Children
for the year 1977-78 is submitted.
Heartfelt thanks and fraternal regards are extended to the Brethren of o ur
California Jurisdicti on for their continued dedication in making possible the endeavors of our Covina Home.
Our children have had an extremely intere ting and meaningful year! June
1978, brought graduation, summer plans, special events, cultural trips, home
visits, and a wide variety of "treats" - including NO summer school1 ! Prior
to June, our residents enjoyed birthday parties, a beautiful Holiday Season and
various special "surprise" trips.
The Fraternity can be proud of the children in our care! As in the case with
all families, our residents have responsibilities to go with the many privileges
they receive. Each one has daily and weekly chores to be completed . These
include bed making , keeping one's room and cottage neat and c lean, waiting
and cleaning tables. serving as guides for our visitors, and most important, getting along with one another.
Our residents are an integral pan of the larger Covina community. Many are
active in Little League, Pop Warner Football. Rainbow, Job's Daughters,
DeMolay. and other community based activities . We also share our facilities
wi th the DeMolay Citrus League Advisory council, Citrus Assembly No . 206
advisors, Bethel 98's choir and guardians, the Happy Hirams Hi-12 annual installation and steak fry. and other Masonic groups. On special occasions. we
also accept invitations for our residents to visit th eir sponsoring Lodges.
This past year has seen o ur Home family enjoying relatively good health. A
few minor accidents have taken place, but we have not suffered any se rious or
prolonged illnesses. We are indebted to Mrs . Ruby Thac ker , our nurse. for her
dedication to keep our children healthy.
Our Masonic Home Alumni Association remains active. ·1wo reunions are
held annually. the Nonhem section meeting the week of Grand Lodge . and the
" All Alumni Annual Picnic ·· being held in the Spring at Covina. April 22. 1978
saw alumni and families numbering 210 enjoying an afternoon and evening of
reminscing, food and fellowship at the Home . We are proud to announce that
Worshipful Master Douglas T. Youngling. King David's Lodge No . 290. F. &
A. M., San Luis Obispo , is an alumnus of Covina. Wor;hipful Doug graduated
in 1962, and needless to say, we are all extremely proud of his accomplishments.
A special acknowledgement is due Brother Ray Howe. our Executive Director. fo r his guidance and leadership this year. We are grateful for the many hours
he has spe nt with us, his suggestions, and his expertise, so wi llingly shared.

Sincerely and fraternally,
JAMES C. BLAl:-IE, Administrator
