REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON
MASONIC SERVICE BUREAUS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Committee on Masonic Service Bureaus is pleased to present the 5lst
Annual Report of its activities for the Masonic year covering the period ending
June 30, 1978.
The nineteen Masonic Service Bureaus are for the purpose of properly relieving the distre;ses of Masons who are members of Lodges in other areas of
California or of Lodges in other Jurisdictions, and their widows and orphans
while residing or visiting in the area of the Masonic Service Bureaus.
The Right Worshipful Donald G. Ingalls, Deputy Grand Master, was appointed Liason Officer to the Committee and we appreciate his support during
the year.
NEW COMMITTEE MEMBER

We welcome G. Basil Bates as a new member of our Committee. He served
the Los Angeles Service Bureau as President and brings to our Committee experience as an administrator.
NEW SECRETARIES

Oliver I. Kitchen replaced Fred R. De Barrows as the Executive Secretary of
the Richmond Bureau. Emery E. Mumford assumed the duties of the Executive
Secretary of the Southern Alameda County Bureau replacing Anthony F. Taylor
who served that Bureau for more than eight years. Both Brothers Kitchen and
Mumford serve their Bureaus without compensation.

166

167

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

MEETINGS

over last year. When compared to a period of seven years ago, the increase is
24 percent, or an average of only a little over 3 percent a year for the seven year
period.

The Committee held four meetings during the year. One was held during
Grand Lodge Week and at that time we had the opportunity to meet with some
of the Officers of the Bureaus.
A meeting was held in June 1978 to review and approve the proposed Budgets
for the nineteen Bureaus.
Two group meetings were held. A meeting in February 1978 was held in
Northern California, and there were sixteen Officers from the Bureaus in that
part of the State in attendance. In March 1978 a meeting was held in Southern
California and there were twenty-one Officers from the Bureaus attending.
During the group meetings, a two-way communication was established, and
the important subjects dealing with the daily operation of the Service Bureau
were discussed in detail. This type of meeting, held early in the year, has proven
very valuable to the new President of the Bureau, as well as all Officers who
attend .
POLICY CHANGE

The Grand Master approved our request to change the Rules and Regulations
for the Operation of the Service Bureaus to reflect the change in the legislation
adopted at the 1977 Annual Communication of Grand Lodge. The Bureaus can
now advance to a needy worthy Brother the sum of $100.00 without the approval
of the Brother's Lodge. The amount was fonnerly $25.00.
BLOOD BANKS

Twelve Bureaus operate Blood Banks for their member Lodges and others.
There were over 2,600 pints of blood donated, and over 2,000 pints given to
our Masonic Brothers and their families during the past year. East Bay and Long
Beach Bureaus were each donated over 350 pints. San Francisco Bureau was
donated 1,650 pints of blood. This is a most worthy Masonic charity that all
Lodges should participate in.
TAXES

Worshipful W. Stanley Davis, Chainnan of the Taxation Committee, has continued to assist our Committee on the important subject of taxation, and we are
grateful for his services and advice.
All Bureaus have filed the required tax reports to both Federal and State
agencies.
The total taxes paid by our Service Bureaus have increased nearly 12 percent
during the past year to a new high of nearly $6,500.00.
BUDGETS

The Budgets for the nineteen Bureaus were reviewed and approved by the
Committee. It is interesting to note that this year, the anticipated cost to operate
the Bureaus was at a new high of $118,000. This is a modest 2 percent increase

BUSH MASONIC RELIEF

The Committee joins with the Officers and members of the six Masoni~ s.erv ice Bureaus located in the Greater Los Angeles Area with deep appreciation
to the Bush Masonic Relief. Their officers are Worshipful Ralph H. Head, President, Most Worshipful Leo E. Anderson, P.G.M. and Most Worshipful Burton
Meyer, Jr., P.G.M.
This Corporation provides the funds to pay for the operating expense for the
six Bureaus. This year, the amount was $65,000, which is 55 percent of the
total budgets for all Bureaus for 1978-1979. The savings to the member Lodges,
who would normally pay a per capita assessment, are of some magnitude and
are appreciated by all. The savings to the member Lodges are used for other
worthwhile Masonic activities.
APPRECIATION

Our Masonic Brothers are enjoying a longer life span, and are traveling more.
California is an attractive place to visit, and as the result, there has been an
acceleration of the needs of sojourning Masons and their families here in
California.
It is through the untiring efforts of the Executive Secretaries that we have a
strong, viable network of Bureaus in this Grand Jurisdiction-the backbone of
a thriving program to assist our sojourners.
As an example, the number of funeral services conducted for sojourners has
increased over 5 percent during the past year. The number of investigations made
by the Bureaus relative to sojourners has increased ~ perc~nt. !he nu~ber of
applications processed to Masonic Homes, both here m California, and mother
jurisdictions has increased 23 percent during the past year.
Probably an ever increasing need to assist sojourning Masons and their .families, together with a continued need to provide various fonns of professional
help, will continue.
Special appreciation is extended to the Grand Master,. the Grand .secretary
and his Staff and to the Chairman of the Taxation Committee for their support
and assistance during the year.
We want to compliment the Presidents, Officers and Committees, and particularly the Executive Secretaries for their excellent ~idance and lead~rship during the past year. The operations of the Bureaus are m the hands of sincere and
devoted Masons.
The Committee has functioned under its budget this past year, and herewith
requests the sum of $1,100.00 to cover expenses during the ensuing year. This
is 21 percent less than requested last year. The details of this requirement have
been furnished the Finance Committee.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON DISTRIBUTION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

After reviewing the Grand Master's Annual Message, the Reports of the
Grand Treasurer, Grand Secretary, Grand Lecturer, Masonic Homes Trustees,
Masonic Homes Endowment Board and the Committee on Masonic Service
Bureaus, the Committee on Distribution submits the following report:
GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE

The Grand Master's Message contains seven decisions and four recommendations. We recommend that the subject matter involved in the Grand Master's
Message be referred to Committees as follows:
Recommendation Number 1, with regard to amending the Cornerstone Laying
Ceremony relative to Hawaii, be referred to the Committees on Jurisprudence,
Ritual and Policy and General Purposes.
Recommendation Number 2, with regard to a Certificate of Membership for
a restored unaffiliated Mason, be referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence.
Recommendation Number 3, with regard to deletion of "Part II Commercialism Regulations relating to Youth Orders" be deleted in its entirety, be
referred to the Committees on Jurisprudence, Policy and General Purposes and
Youth Committee.
Recommendation Number 4, with regard to use of emblems and insignia by
clandestine Lodges be closely monitored, and if necessity arise, appropriate
action be taken to prohibit the unauthorized use of our emblems or insignia, be
referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence, Policy and General Purposes and
Foreign Recognition Committee.
Decision Number l, with regard to conducting a Constitution Ceremony of
a Lodge for Master Masons only and not as a public ceremony, be referred to
the Committees on Jurisprudence, Policy and General Purposes and Ritual.
Decision Number 2, with regard to Section 160 of the California Masonic
Code relevent to a Resolution presented to Grand Lodge at two consecutive
Annual Communications and involving a "Carry Over Vote," be referred to
the Committee on Jurisprudence.
Decision Number 3, with regard to permitting a Stated Meeting to be convened by someone other than the Master or Wardens of the Lodge, be referred
to the Committees on Jurisprudence and Policy and General Purposes.
Decision Number 4, with regard to the Resolution entitled "Master Mason
Proficiency-3rd Degree" adopted by the Grand Lodge at the 1977 Annual
Communication and applicable to all Masters and Wardens installed on or after
July l, 1978, be referred to the Committees on Jurisprudence, Policy and
General Purposes and Ritual.

GRAND TREASURER'S REPORT

We recommend that this report be referred in its entirety to the Committee
on Finance.
GRAND SECRETARY'S REPORT

We recommend that this report be referred to the Committees as follow:
l. That portion relating to changes of meeting place, be referred to the
Committee on Charters and By-Laws.
2. That portion relating to consolidation of Lodges, be referred to the Committee on Charters.
<JRAND LECTURER'S REPORT

We recommend that the portion of the report dealing with the 1978-79
budget, be referred to the Committee on Finance.
MASONIC HOMES TRUSTEES' REPORT

We recommend that this report, be referred in its entirety to the Committee
on Finance.
MASONIC HOMES ENDOWMENT BOARD

We recommend that this report, be referred in its entirety to the Committee
on Finance.
REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON MASONIC SERVICE BUREAUS

We recommend that the portion of the report dealing with budget, be referred
to the Committee on Finance.
Respectfully submitted,
GEORGE E. FRANK, Chairman
GARY A. BAUMAN
RALPH H. JOHNSTON

MORNING SESSION-Tuesday, October 10, 1978

Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "Yes" vote .

Grand Lodge was called on at 9:30 A.M.·, the Grand Master presiding . Grand
Lodge was raised by William T. Johnson, Master of Greenleaf Lodge No. 670,
and Dennis Spruitt, Master of Azure Lodge No. 533. Gavels used during the
Morning Session were presented to the Grand Master by Lodi Lodge No. 256,
Moreno Valley Lodge No . 804, San Pedro Lodge No. 332, the I 18th and 160th
Masonic Districts, Indian Wells Valley Lodge No . 691, the 500th Masonic
District, Ionic Lodge No . 520, and the East Bay Masters and Wardens
Association.
The Very Reverend William W. Widenham, Grand Chaplain delivered the
Invocation . The minutes of the morning and afternoon sessions of Monday,
October 9, 1978 were read and approved .

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
When holdover Resolution No. I to require the reading of the biographical
sketch of the recommendee for the office of Junior Grand Warden immediately
prior to the election of the Junior Grand Warden was presented to Grand Lodge
in 1977, we stated to Grand Lodge that in our opinion the legislation submitted
by the proponents was sufficient to carry out the intent of the proponents and
we repeat this statement.
Adopted by 2/3 vote.

UNFINISHED BUSINESS (1977)
Election - Junior Grand Warden (See 1977 Proceedings , p. 221)
Changes to Masonic Funeral Service (See 1977 Proceedings, p. 252)

RESOLUTIONS
The Resolutions presented for consideration at the 1978 Annual Communication were referred by the Grand Master to the various Grand Lodge Committees as noted. The reports on each and the action taken by Grand Lodge are
shown below the Resolution. The titles of those Resolutions which were withdrawn are listed following those on which action was taken.

ELECTION-JUNIOR GRAND WARDEN
(1977-Resolution No. 4)
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes favors this Resolution which
directs the Grand Master to read the biographical sketch of the recommendee
for the office of Junior Grand Warden immediately prior to the election and to
introduce him if he be present.
This Committee's opinion, expressed last year, was brief, and so I quote it
to you now:

"Although Section 200 C.M.C. provides the means for dissemination of
the name of the recommendee for Junior Grand Warden, your Committee on
Policy and General Purposes believes that there is merit in Resolution No. 4.

CHANGES TO MASONIC FUNERAL SERVICE
(1977 - Resolution No. 27)
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This resolution proposes "That the autonomous authority of the Grand Lecturer and/or the Ritual Committee be subject to the same review as is now required of the Grand Master in decisions made by him during his term of office"
and that the recent changes in the funeral service " instituted by the Grand Lecturer be reviewed by Grand Lodge at its next Annual Communication and either
approved or rescinded by vote of the members present.' '
The highest office that can be bestowed upon a Master Mason in this Jurisdiction is that of Grand Master, and Section 1052 CMC requires that every official act , decision or recommendation made by the Grand Master be reported
at the Annual Colillmunication of Grand Lodge for its approval or disapproval.
Since Grand Lodge requires this of the Grand Master, then should not Grand
Lodge require the same of the Grand Lecturer?
The responsibility of the Committee on Ritual as custodian of the esoteric
work (Section 1235 CMC) obviously is to maintain conformity to and uniformity
in the work. Nothing tends to destroy uniformity more quickly than frequent
changes.
Section 1114- lst CMC states in part: "It shall be the duty of the Grand
Lecturer to require conformity with the ADOPTED ritual and work."
This brings us to a crucial question. Does the Ritual Committee have the
authority to make changes of the kind contained in the letters of November 1,
1976, and June 1, 1977, ordering changes in the Funeral Service without the
approval of the Grand Lodge?
We have carefully considered our law and our past practice. As a result , we
conclude that the action taken is not in accord with either.
We have considered California Masonic Code Sections 2690, 1114 and 1235
among others. We have also considered past editions of Ross Digest and the
proceedings of Grand Lodge for many years, from 1928 through 1977.
We have carefully considered the possibility of a distinction between ritual
and ceremony , or ritual and floorwork.
The history of our ceremonies is that they have been established by the Grand
Lodge and changed by the Grand Lodge. Past Grand Lecturers have referred to
our ceremonies as ritual . The California Masonic Code states that only the Grand

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

172

Lodge can authorize a change in our ritual. It says nothing about ceremonies.
This is no oversight. They have always been regarded as ritual.
As to fioorwork, when we consider all the printed footnotes, directions and
instructions by which we must abide as a part of our rital, there appears to be
no question but that fioorwork is a part of ritual .
At the 1955 Annual Communication, Elbert W. Davis, Grand Lecturer, and
the Committee on Ritual recommended and presented to Grand Lodge proposed
changes in the Funeral Service containing 13 numbered footnotes relating to
instructions for the Master's movements and fioorwork ( 1955 Proceedings, pages
224 - 230). The entire Funeral Service, including these 13 instructional footnotes, was adopted by Grand Lodge.
At the 1976 Annual Communication, H. Douglas Lemons, Grand Lecturer,
and the Committee on Ritual recommended that the Grand Lodge Ceremony for
presentation of 50 year Veterans Buttons be completely rewritten and Grand
Lodge approved the recommendation.
At the 1977 Annual Communication, the Grand Lecturer presented to Grand
Lodge proposed changes in the Golden Veterans Award ~ontain!ng thr~e paragraphs of preamble of instructions and 11 footnotes relating to mstructJ.ons for
the Master's movements and fioorwork (1977 Proceedings, pages 213 - 215).
The entire ceremony, including the preamble and the 11 instructional footnotes,
was adopted by Grand Lodge.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes is convinced by the provisions
of our law and the practices of the Ritual Committee and Grand Lecturers in the
past that:
I. The Ritual referred to in Section 2690 of the California Masonic Code
includes all ceremonies, including the Funeral Service.
2. That any proposed revisions, corrections or additions to our Ritual, including all ceremonies, monitors and books of instructions, require the approval of the Grand Lodge.
It is the caretully considered judgment of your Committee on Policy and General Purposes that this Resolution should be approved.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes, therefore, recommends a
"Yes" vote.
The Committee on Jurisprudence:

When Resolution No. 27 to require Grand Lodge approval of changes in our
Funeral Service was reported to Grand Lodge in 1977, the Committee on Policy
and General Purposes and the Committee on Jurisprudence agreed that the Ritual
referred to in Section 2690 includes all of the Grand Lodge Ceremonies, including the Funeral Service.
Therefore, in order to carry this Resolution into effect Section 2690 must be
amended by inserting after the word "immemorial" the words "or to make any
changes in any ceremony of this Grand Lodge, including the Funeral Service."
To place this legislation before Grand Lodge we move the adoption of the
above legislation .
Not Adopted.

CREDIT UNION - COMMITTEE TO STUDY
FEASIBILITY
(1)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & AM. of California:

WHEREAS, Resolution No . 33 at the 1977 Grand Communication dealt with
the need for help on behalf of impoverished Lodges, and while the intent of the
proposal was considered worthy, the measure was rejected as not being the
proper answer to the need; and
WHEREAS, a suggestion that a credit union of .a non-profit nature, f?rmed
within the framework of Masonry might better provide for these needs, without
arbitrarily imposing an additional burden upon the membership; and
WHEREAS, thi!f proposal has been investigated at some depth and discussed
with many Masons of the Sacramento, California area, eliciting many favorable
comments; and
WHEREAS, the few objections thereto appear to be surmountable with little
or no difficulty; and
WHEREAS, such a credit union would promote thrift among the Fraternity;
would provide a better place of deposit for the funds of Lodges, Tem~le Boards
and individual Masons at a favorable rate of interest; would make possible better
conditions of financing the activities and needs of individual Masons, Lodges
and Temple Boards at a favorable rate of interest; would tend to reduce the
demands on Lodge welfare funds, by increasing thrift among the members;
would lend confidence in the ability of Temple Boards to succeed in their efforts
to provide better housing for the Lodge, thus encouraging donations and/or share
purchasing; would enhance the ability of Masons to contribute to the support of
the Masonic Homes, by tending to increase their financial worth.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, this Grand Lodge assembly of
Masons, calls for the appointment of a Grand Lodge Committee composed of
Masons, knowledgeable in the field of finance, with particular reference to the
operation of credit unions, to make an in-depth study of the benefits to be obtained from such an organization and also to develop ways and means of
overcoming any objectionable features that may be found, and render a comprehensive report to the Grand Master, with copies to Finance and other

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Committees of the Grand Lodge affected thereby . That a copy of the final report
be made available to all Constituent Lodges not later than February 1, 1979,
said report to include the recommendations of the Committee.

The Committee on Finance:
Resolution No. 1 proposes the formation of a Special Committee to make an
in-depth study of credit unions in order to render a report as to the feasibility
of forming such an association within the framework of Masonry.
Before responding directly to this Resolution, let us explore briefly the organization of a credit union. Our source for this information is the State of California, Department of Corporations, the agency charged with the responsibility
of the administration of the California Credit Union Law, and the California
Credit Union League, an association of independent credit unions in California.
A credit union is a legal entity which may be organized under either State or
Federal law, by and for people who already have a common bond. The members
become owners through the purchase of shares. They agree to save their money
in a facility they own and operate, a credit union, and to make their collective
savings available for low cost loans to all members.
By and large, credit union loans are personal loans for provident or productive
purposes. Normal reasons for borrowing include old bills, taxes, medical expenses, autos, vacations, household items, educations, weddings, and family
emergencies. In some places, credit unions are permitted to make mortgage loans
when surplus funds are available, but this should not be the normal practice of
a credit union, because it involves a long term debt.
It should be noted that since a credit union is a cooperative organization, its
officials are volunteers and may not be compensated, but there will be necessary
administration costs.
A credit union can do business only with its members. A proper balance of
investors and borrowers is necessary to insure its success.
The proponent of Resolution No. 1 indicates that such a credit union could
receive funds from and make loans to Lodge and Temple Boards, as well as
individuals. The printed information at hand did not define any type membership
except individuals. The Department of Corporations stated that under certain
circumstances organizations, parent to the common bond factor, were allowed
to become members of credit unions. They noted that each group applying for
a credit union charter must submit a set of By-Laws defining its membership
and outlining the scope of its activity. The Department further indicated that
certain restrictions were placed on organization membership. One being that
they could not bo"ow more than the value of the shares they owned in the credit
union. This limitation is not placed on individual members. They also stated that
each application for a credit union charter must also be approved by the Internal
Revenue Service and the Franchise Tax Board.
While your Committee on Finance has presented the foregoing information
to resolve the question of whether it could be done, the relevant question is,
should it be done? Is it wise to create any fund within the structure of Masonry
which would make personal loans to its members and create a situation which
might entice an individual into our Fraternity for monetary reasons? We believe
that many Masons already have the opportunity to belong to a credit union and
the mechanics and cost of administering a credit union covering all of California
and Hawaii could be insurmountable.
A credit union fails to enhance the true objectives of Freemasonry and could
only lead to an interruption of the peace and harmony which we now possess
and continue to strive for.

Respectfully submitted,
J. H. LEINEKE, JW No. 795
Referred to the Committees on Policy and General Purposes, Jurisprudence
and Finance.
The Committee on Policy a'nd General Purposes:
Resolution No. l proposes that a Grand Lodge Committee be appointed to
make a comprehensive report to the Grand Master not later than February l,
1979, of the feasibility of establishing a Credit Union. The proponent envisions
investors who would be individual Masons, Lodges and Temple Associations
who would receive ''favorable rates of interest.'' The borrowers in tum would
be Masons, Lodges and Temple Boards.
If, as your Committee assumes from the whereases and resolve clause of this
Resolution, the proposed Credit Union would be under the auspices, direction
and control of the Grand Lodge, the Committee believes it is not and should not
be the policy of this Grand Lodge.
We recognize the need to consider new ideas which may be of benefit to the
Grand Lodge, to Lodges and to Masons. However, that consideration should be
limited when it conflicts with the policies, purposes and concept of this Grand
Lodge.
One policy of the Grand Lodge is that it is not and should not be involved
in banking or insurance. The reputation of the Fraternity is too important to
allow it to be involved in such commercial ventures. Hence the use of the name
of the Grand Lodge or Masonic or Masonry in such a venture would have to be
disapproved.
As a matter of policy and our Masonic law, the question of authority to invest
in a Credit Union would have to be carefully investigated. If such an organization
could not properly be connected with the Grand Lodge could such an organization qualify as an institution in which Lodges might invest?
Nothing in this report should be construed as preventing any group of Brothers
from conducting their own investigation. They would need to determine whether
such an organization would prosper without using the name of Masonry, whether
it could exist where no employer is able to pour in deductions from salary authorized by members, and what benefits there could be to Lodges and to Masons
generally not already available through existing financial institutions. While
these answers are needed, the basic objections to connection with the Grand
Lodge are so strong that the investigators should not be a Grand Lodge
Committee.
We recommend a "No" vote.
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
The Committee on Jurisprudence reported that the language submitted by the
proponent was adequate to accomplish the purpose of the Resolution .

GRAND ORATION
PRESERVING OUR FRATERNAL FOUNDATIONS
MELVIN F. SCHUSTER, Grand Orator
Most Worshipful Grand Master and my Brethren of the Grand Lodge:
To stand at this podium to address you, my Brethren, is a privilege and honor
which far surpasses my wildest expectations. I sincerely thank you for your most
courteous reception and trust that the thoughts which you allow me to share with
you this afternoon will in some small way contribute to the significance of this
Communication and perhaps merit your consideration as we set out to do that
work which we came here to do.
To begin with, Most Worshipful, to you I express my deepest appreciation
for the opportunity you gave to me last year to serve our Grand Lodge and I
could never, never put into words my thanks for the courtesies and considerations given to me by you during our sojourns throughout the State with the Grand
Family. I also want to take advantage of this moment to acknowledge the fraternal devotion of my fellow Grand Lodge Officers; and to the Masters and
Wardens sitting here today and through them to the Brethren of this great Jurisdiction, my profound gratitude for the numberless acts of kindness by which
they have made me eternally their debtor. My life and that of my wife, Peggy,
has been made that much richer and more meaningful by the privilege of our
associations with you.
October, that delightful month of the year signifying the harvest time, finds
us again assembled in our Annual Communication to exchange fraternal salutations, to give an accounting of our stewardship, to listen to the wise counsel
of our master wprkmen, to enjoy, for much too short a span of time, the fellowship of our Brethren, to pay tribute to the memory of our departed Brethren
who came so often into these chambers but who will enter no more, and then,
as Masons have done in all ages before us, discuss the business of the Grand
Lodge and go forth from this place to pursue our labors for the benefit of our
noble Craft.
At this particular time it is my duty to address you ''upon matters appertaining
to the Craft," and fully realizing the many former moments of eloquence, I most
humbly implore your indulgence.
At the Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge we concern ourselves with
the effort to chart our course of future activities, constantly bearing in mind the
necessity for a strong hand on that tiller which will guide the ship of California
Masonry.
We often hear some of our Brethren expound at great length on the fact that
we are not greatly interested in the past, that our chief concern is not even with
the present, but that our efforts should concern themselves only with the future.
I submit to you, my Brethren, that we cannot intelligently plan the future of this
or any other institution, and that we cannot determine the correct paths of wisdom in the present unless we shall have first analyzed that which has taken place
in the past; for it is the experiences of the days gone by that must serve as guides
to our actions in the future. As the sands in the hour-glass of life fall toward the
bottom of the vessel, I find myself irresistably moving with what I consider that
ever-increasing group of Brethren who believe that the area of their greatest

179

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

usefullness is to be found in trying to solve the problems of the present and
preparing for those of the future. The yesterdays were full of interest, but today
and the days ahead are filled with the inspiration of anticipated success. Therefore I trust I may be forgiven if, in the brief time alloted to me, I might discuss
my feelings on matters of dismay and concern, but yet of hope and encouragement which confront us as members of our Institution and which I would hope
merit your thoughts and deliberations.
Our society in general is witnessing an era of restlessness, and the effects are
being felt by Masonry as well as other institutions.
Men of equal abilities, intellect and learning, espouse opposite political, economic and religious programs. Men of equal character champion as ethical and
condemn as immoral the very same practice. The totalitarian states differ as
bitterly with each other as with the democracies.
All of these strivings and confusions show that mankind is searching, probing,
questing for surer collective foundations; during the process they make even
more imperative the need for surer individual foundations.
In the midst of this confusion we frequently encounter agitated and excited
Brethren who have lost some of their hospitality for the traditional conception
of Masonry's sphere of action. We easily notice these Brethren, for they run
through the hallowed halls of Masonry pointing the proverbial finger at those
activities to which, in their opinion, the fraternity should commit itself and also
to nebulous opportunities of which it might fail to avail itself.
Personally, I have to admit that I am slow to sanction the innovations proposed
by our enthusiastic Brethren because I strongly feel that they may have fallen
victims to a confusion of thought leading them to impose upon the Institution,
duties or activities which are in conflict with the real purpose and meaning of
Craft Masonry!
In another apartment of our Temple can be heard the clamor of concern for
our so-called decline in membership. Our Grand Master, in his address to this
august body, has sufficiently explained the statistics which tend to support this
clamor. However, the point is well taken, and decline, justified or not, should
be of great concern to us!
And still elsewhere, my Brethren, the attentive ear will detect rumblings of
deep concern for Masonry's effectiveness in our educational system, in our communities and even our individual Lodges.
Ask the superintendent or master worlcman of any large construction site
which part of the building required the most deliberate and exacting labor and
he will most assuredly answer, "The foundation." The foundation ... that portion of the structure usually unseen and often unappreciated. There are five separate foundations to which I wish to address my remarks of the afternoon.
We are builders!! Our heritage flows down through history from the ancient
artisans in stone. How long their magnificient cathedrals stood was solely dependent upon the foundation upon which they were built. We are builders in
another sense, for we construct, shape and mold from an inquisitive candidate,
a Master Mason!
How that Master Mason functions is going to be based upon how we set his
foundation and guide him in erecting the superstructure of his Masonic life . Just
as the height of a building is limited to its foundation, so is the candidate's

spiritual height based on his foundations; for this man on whom we confer the
Third Degree is no longer simply, Mr. Jones. He is John Jones, Master Mason.
But even beyond that, he is your Lodge. He is Masonry!
This new Masonic career will follow him all over the globe and his effectiveness as an example of our noble Craft begins in the northeast corner of the
Lodge room. How appropriate that it should be at the point, midway between
north and east, a reminder of the fact that a traveler has left darkness and has
moved towards the light. True, some of the darkness still clings to him; as yet
he belongs in part to the north . But he is turning his face eastward; he is striving
for light and truth.
Why is the lesson of the northeast corner such a pinnacle experience in the
Masonic life of a man? Because there the essential dignity of the individual is
emphasized in a manner that is unforgettable. With body erect and head held
high he stands proud to be recognized as a creature of the Great Architect. At
that moment he is the most important man in the entire Masonic Craft. Worlcing
tools are placed in his hands. His preparatory period of life now under way, he
is ready to enter upon its serious business, ready to begin his labors on a Temple
not made with hands.
And since a man receives the degrees but once, he will never stand in the
northeast corner as the youngest Entered Apprentice again . Never, therefore,
should we let him forget that once he stood there, nor why!
The guidance he receives from that point on will determine whether he becomes a Mason or simply a member of a Masonic Lodge.
Freemasonry is what Freemasons are when, and only when, it is seen in action. As one writer in the "Masonic Herald" puts it, "I would not give much
for your Freemasonry unless it is seen in everyday life. Lamps do not talk though
they do shine. A ijghthouse sounds no drums nor beats any gongs, yet far over
the water its friendly glow of light is seen by the captain. So let your light so
shine and be recognized by the image of your life as to illustrate and exemplify
your conduct and it shall not fail to be illustrious.''
The goal of an illustrious life? My Brethren, it is possible for us to achieve
this goal, but our work must begin outside the West Gate. Once we relax our
standards ever so little, a long and difficult struggle is ahead before their lofty
position can be regained, if ever.
One of the most important responsibilities any Worshipful Master will have,
is the selection of his Investigating Committees on petitions for membership.
No petitioner has an inherent right to become a Freemason; it is a privilege that
may be granted or denied according to the worthiness or unworthiness of the
man who applies. Sometimes it is our duty to object. Why not get a "pool" of
good, conscientious Brethren who will really investigate, leaving no stone unturned? It isn't enough merely to say "He has never been in trouble; there's no
reason why he should not be admitted to our fellowship ." I prefer to know
whether there is any good reason why he SHOULD be admitted. Just because
he has managed thus far to keep out of trouble with the law is hardly what we
could call a positive recommendation.
"Bring the standard back to the line," the commanding officer in one of the
Napoleonic wars ordered in a message to the boy who carried the regimental
banner. But the lad was on fire with zeal for victory.

178

181

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

"Bring the line up to the standard," he urged his chief. That is our challenge
at the West Gate.
I'm sure many of you have heard comments from our Brethren such as, "They
do nothing but confer degrees.'' If our Lodge Officers do nothing but repeat ~he
words and phrases of our ritual, then the critics have a point. But if in the process
of conferring degrees our Lodges are making Masons, then their criticism is
entirely unfounded. It all depends on what precedes, what accompanies and what
follows the ritualistic ceremonies of our degrees.
Is this a familiar situation? You' re disappointed in a certain newly raised
Brother named Fred. Fred was impatient to get his petition into your Lodge,
then impatient to get the degrees over. You were a little unhappy that the candidate was permitted to get by on somewhat poor proficiency work between
degrees. The result was that he came. to Lodge exactly three times and you haven't seen him since. Having used the degrees as a stepping stone, he rushed
on to whatever it was he wanted in the first place. Perhaps the thought occurred
to you that he would have been better off and certainly Masonry would be better
off if he had joined the Elm Street Social Club.
But let's take a closer look at that situation for a moment. First, the Lodge
didn't have to elect Fred to membership if that appeared to be his motive. Second, the Lodge didn't have to rush through the degrees. In doing so, didn't it
act as an accessory?
If the Lodge had required that Fred take the time to start learning what Freemasonry is all about before the degrees, during the degrees, and after the degrees
he just might have become a Master Mason in the truest sense of the word.
Conrad Hahn, a noted Masonic scholar, once wrote, "Unfortunately the rapid
process of the individual from one degree to another continues, with an appalling
dearth of Masonic education and enlightenment between the degrees. No wonder
the ritual work is regarded less and less as a mystic experience to inspire a man
and to improve his heart and mind for the art of living.
I share the opinion that the lack of educational work in the average Lodge is
the principal reason for the loss of interest and the consequent poor attendance
in Masonry. A Lodge of Master Masons does not exist for the purpose of furnishing members for other organizations. Its purpose is to make Master Masons.
Why, then, shouldn't we take the time to do just that?
If a Lodge has no time to ripen a candidate, to mold him, to give him a firm
foundation, to give him good and wholesome instruction before it raises him to
the Sublime Degree, it won't find time to do it after he signs the By-Laws. Do
you think you can get the average new member to come back to Lodge for such
educational experiences when you didn't require them between the degrees? Of
course not!
In our symbolism we have a commodity which no else in the world possesses.
Think of what a businessman would do if he held in his grasp a product that was
one of a kind and which was in demand by the consumer. Don't you think he'd
lash out with a sales campaign to end all sales campaigns? We have such a
product and we need no sales campaign because men come to us thirsting for
the knowledge that only we can provide! All too often the thirsty candidate
comes to a dry well!
It is Masonry's great function to inform; it is the function of individual Masons

to perform. How do we judge our performance? By what standard do we measure
our effectiveness? Can it be determined by the esteem with which we are regarded in our local communities? Answer this question then, "How much would
your Lodge be missed by the community tomorrow if it ceased to exist tonight'?"
The reputation of the Fraternity, to a greater or lesser degree, is in the keeping
of the individual Mason. It is within the power of every Brother to glorify or
nullify the institution. The general public never reads Masonic books nor Masonic philosophy. Its idea of the fraternity is not well defined, and the sole basis
of judgment it falls back upon, is the character of the men who are supposed
to exemplify its teachings. It isn't the Grand Master; it isn't the Grand Lodge,
it isn't even your Lodge-it is you. If you want Masonry to remain a vibrant
force only you can make it to be that way.
From time immemorial, our Craft has exercised an influence over our society
that has been due to its continuing attachment to unchallengeable, fundamental
principles of human conduct. In short, the foundations laid long ago still support
the superstructure of our civil society.
But new roads are opening to us; new designs on the trestleboard to be tested;
new experiments proposed which challenge our curiosity and our daring. If ever
we needed individuals conscious of the basic principles upon which our institution was founded, it is now! Our local communities, our school boards, our
State and Federal governing bodies are crying out for the leadership dedicated
to old fashioned Americanism.
The society of our day supports numberless institutions and organizations,
each especially created and designed to advance one particular science, to promote one particular profession, to encourage one particular business or industry,
to protect one particular group of labor, to uphold the interests of one particular
church or party .• In those organizations the Mason has a wonderful opportunity
to bring to the treatment of every problem and activity of our times, an application of the sound principles which Masonry has instilled into his consciousness
and into the impulses of his life. There, in the everyday world, my Brethren,
is our opportunity to win the world to that Masonry of action and spirit which
is the very heart-beat of civilization.
We hear much about our schools, but do we listen? The Masonic Fraternity
is on record as a champion of public education. There is not one among us who
would care to take a backward step. In a nation such as ours it is imperative that
the people should be educated. We stand always, and with all our strength, for
the protection, integrity and upbuilding of the public school system. In that we
are unanimous. The individual Mason is not committed by reason of such loyalty
to specific measures of education. I do not conceive it to be my Masonic duty
blindly to endorse every measure presented to me, merely because it comes from
those who have in charge the administration of the schools. I do not recognize
it as a Masonic duty to vote for issues of school bonds, for instance, unless I
have assured myself of the public necessity therefor. The point I wish to make
is this-that Masons should never become the unquestioning and unreasoning
bond-servants of any institution, whether schools, or churches, or societies.
Frankly, as a parent, I'm concerned!! Law enforcement agencies report that
the incidence and severity of crimes committed by youths are increasing ... suicide
attempts both successful and unsuccessful are on an upswing. The number of

teenage pregnancies is increasing each year at a dramatic rate. The misuse of
alcohol and other drugs by young people shows no evidence of abatement. The

bored with everything except the pursuit of "Fun" and they are at once apathetic

Our immediate inclination is to ask, "What is wrong with our young people?"
Why do they reject our values of hard work, self-determination and sacrifice of

When standards, whatever they may be, if imposed, are not rigidly enforced,

With an increasing frequency young couples are living together without getting
married and without the disapproval of their peers.
Many responsible and concerned parents buy and encourage the use of birthcontrol pills because sexual activity is condoned by current social standards, and
parents feel helpless to do anything about it. . . unwilling to impose their ideas
on their own children.
Young people need and want authority in their lives. The absence or weakness
of such authority contributes to the lack of purpose which is characteristic of too
many of our young adults.
With the understanding and support of parents and the rest of the community,
the school can help to make some changes. There is increasing evidence that
many people are looking for a return to more structure in our schools for stricter
discipline and for more rigidly enforced standards of achievemen;. We must
have open communication between the parents, the schools and the community.
That foundation stone of our country's greatness must not be chipped,
cracked, scratched or or marred by negativism, complacency or disinterest. It
is our duty to know what we are doing when we exercise the electoral franchise,
and to realize that those who administer human institutions are as human as
ourselves, subject to the same ambitions and faults . There is never a time when
Masons should not be particularly careful to see that the causes they publicly
support have real merit and deserve such support.
There is yet another foundation I wish for you to consider; our families. We
are hearing a lot today about having the wives and families participating more
in Masonic activities-and that is good!
When Masonry was first established in this country during the early Colonial
period, its rapid growth and popularity could be attributed greatly to the need
for an interest and activity; some place for men to gather. -Other than going to
church on Sunday, there was little activity in those early days for a man to get
fellowship with other men .
We teach and advocate close family ties . We certainly never would recommend that a man not be with his wife and children. We want our members to
be good husbands and devoted fathers, but in our zeal to make our Lodge successful, we too often will require so much of our officers and Brethren that we
command more of their time than their families get. This particularly is harmful
in younger families. We should consider revising our schedules and requirements

so that a young man can serve as an officer without imposing too much on the
time needed for and by his family.
What I am pointing out is that Masonry needs to be more considerate and
smarter in involving the women insofar as is possible. We should have more
joint activites for husbands and wives and families-special dinners, picnics,
trips, and a host of other opportunities that are available .
.
There is much that can be done to interest and cause any wife to want her
husband to be an active Mason so she can enjoy such activities with him. If she
does become interested and excited, she well can be a tremendous public relations force, a powerful publicity agent, and a goodwill ambassador for our
Fraternity instead of being a grumbling and unhappy "Masonic widow·" (A
term I find distasteful)
Show me a Lodge that has the family involved in its activities, and I'll show
you an active, vibrant force in the community.
Let me cite an example. On October 30th of last year, your Grand Lodge
Officers traveled to Los Molinos for the purpose of laying the Cornerstone for
the new Temple of Molino Lodge No. 150, a Lodge with a membership of 144.
On that particular day the wives of the Brethren along with members of the
local Chapter of the Eastern Star provided a pot-luck dinner for over 650 people.
I like to think they all came to hear the oration of the afternoon, but I'm not so
naive as to realize that the entire community came to share in the joy and pride
of Molino Lodge.
There is yet one additional theme upon which we might contemplate.
Let's take a closer look at the situation of membership and Lodge attendance.
I mention both in the same context since one is a function of the other. Throughout our country most fraternal organizations are experiencing a drop in the total
number of memllers. I am not wont to quote figures for you're well aware that
statistics on one side of the ledger are equally germane on the other.
Any number of reasons are offered; the lure of television, the fear of cri.me
in our urban areas, the fact that we do not solicit membership, the weakening
of moral attitudes and religious and cultural interests.
On the other hand, organizations of strictly a social nature are witnessing a
growth in members, partially due to the fact that they are offering anything that
enough members want to do. So the casual observer would ~unnise t~a~ those
groups that major in social activity advance, and the more staid, moralistic bodies decline.
However, there is another facet of this jewel of contention to consider. There
are many who would equate these social organizations with Freemasonry as one
and the same type of institution. They are definite~y not! N~ matter ~ow i><:rsonally gratifying they may be to their members with the philanthropic, social
or insurance programs, they are not "fraternal" organizations by definition. ,,
The Latin word "frater" from which we derive "fraternal" means "brother,
and it is not defined in terms of social endeavors or philanthropy but it is defined
in terms of the mutual obligations and responsibilty of Brotherhood. The fellowship of social activity and the "Good works" of a philanthropic project are
a part of the character of a fraternity but, for there to be a fraternity in any real
sense of the word, there must be the invisible, enduring, voluntarily assumed
obligation of brotherhood!

184

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

I have to unwillingly concede that in today's culture, some men find the ethical
and moral implications of true fraternalism too subtle and too lacking in immediate realization to hold their interest. They would prefer the instant gratification of fun or applied philanthropy; of collecting money, or selling tickets to
raise money for a particular project to help other people-and this is good-but
this is not the point. The point is that applied philanthropy has very little to do
with that quality of brotherhood contemplated in the Degrees of Freemasonry.
Whoa now! Before you shout out, "What about charity?" let me continue.
The true fraternalism of Masonry is invisible, something sensed rather than expressed, a noble emotion that is enduring and voluntary. No one forces an individual to assume the obligations of our Craft. Only a mature man, who acts
of his own free will and accord, can take on the responsibilities of Masonry; to
first undertake and then perform the duties of brotherhood and pledge himself
to the life long practice of Brotherly Love, Relief and Truth .
If Masonry is so good, why do we not have men standing in line awaiting
admission? Why are the Lodge rooms not packed to the rafters when the Master
asks the Junior Deacon to invite the Brethren in? Though I am able to solve the
most complex problems submitted by Wor. Bro. Ralph Head in his quarterly
challenges appearing in the "California Freemason," I confess, my Brethren,
I do not have the solution to the issue before us. The simple answers of television, crime and cultural weaknesses are too simple. They're not answers at
all; merely excuses.
It doesn't require any extensive research to realize that in the last two decades
our society has undergone a frightening upheaval. Attitudes toward ethics and
religion are almost beyond recognition . Attitudes toward the family, the home,
and the country have changed. Regardless of what Chevrolet's advertising men
tell us, even hot dogs, baseball and apple pie are slipping!
And Masonry, with its simple belief that its teachings and principles can make
good men better, has fewer takers now than in the past. Part of the reason is
sadly apparent. Today's young man has no compelling desire to be better. In
his own mind he is good enough, just doing his own thing. Following in Dad's
footsteps is not a "tum-on" to him. Even the curious are no longer curious and
the ambitious (let's face it, there are some) no longer find the economic advantage of Masonic membership worth the cost. So much for petitioners!
To me, what is even more frightening is that the prevailing social changes are
not confined to the "young people ." The sad truth is that many of the elders
have followed the piping of the young and have accepted the new values and
the new morality as an excuse for self-indulgence. Even our Masonry has been
affected by this changing moral outlook because Masons are people. To some,
our ritual is boring; the once impressively binding nature of our obligations has
been rationalized to mere esoterics. Sure, they pay their dues but their one responsibility to the Craft appears to be providing those vacant seats at our
meetings.
Since I have proposed the problem, you are well within your right to demand
of me a solution or solutions! Unfortunately, they cannot be neatly counted off
in numerical order because the best answers lie within the breasts of each of us .
We are told that Freemasonry has emerged stronger from every adverse

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

185

condition that has confronted it, because the Brethren answered the challenge
by returning to the basics of the Fraternity .

But must we have a crisis before every member becomes as aware of Freemasonry's tenets as he is aware of yesterday's ball scores?
Must we have another world war or another era of anti-Masonic haranguing
and propaganda before every Brother is challenged to go forth into the community and show of what Masons are really made?
The time of adversity is now! The foundation upon which we must build solidarity in our Order, the practice of our moral responsibilities and the perfection
of the practice of Brotherly Love is awaiting our fervant labor.
In 1969, there appeared in an issue of The Indiana Freemason an article,
titled "A Modern Fable of the Builders." Though almost IO years old the content is as appropriate today as it was at that time.
"Once upon a time there were some God-fearing men who, after consulting
with one another many times, agreed to build a temple or tower to the glory of
the Grand Architect of the Universe. Its foundation stones were Brotherly Love,
Relief and Truth; and its gates Temperance, Fortitude, Prudence and Justice. Its
doors opened on three steps where the apprentices learned the building arts and,
when proficient, became master workmen skilled in all trades.
"In spite of divisions of opinion and ill-wishers, the work progressed and the
enterprise succeeded. Even the profane grudgingly admitted the structure was
well grounded and of benefit to men.
"To help continue the building, other workers of good report were allowed
to join in the tasks . Then the ranks of workers swelled continually .
"Time passed and some of the workers said, 'Go to; we must beautify the
building for the benefit of the workers and the admiration of men.'
"So they con~eived additions to the fundamental structure. Pointing out that
the original building plans were incomplete and some lost, they persuaded a few
more of the workers to labor on building superstructures. To enhance these 'improvements,' planning committees were organized and the leaders assumed magnificent titles such as Mighty Pandjorum, Supreme Pooh Bah, Grand Wizard,
Imperial Popover, etc . Each designed rooms befitting his ambitions, and soon
the great building acquired bays, ells, gables and minarets never conceived by
its founders. These committees also divided themselves into smaller parties and
vied with each other as to who should be the greatest.
"All this naturally resulted in less labor on the original temple, and the building suffered thereof from lack of workers.
"However, as others noted the apparent success of the 'beautifying,' they
became enamored of more and greater 'beauties.' Thus, the temple progress
seemed stymied, and the labor on the original temple seemed dull to some.
''So it was proposed by a few that another addition be built to top all others
where fun and amusement would reign supreme. These grotesque additions became a subject of merriment to outsiders as well as a burden on the walls of the
original temple where time began to take its toll .
"All the various improvements, additions and beautifications having run their
course and with human nature being what it is, some of the additions were not
able to stand the wear of time and loss of vitality. So a day of reckoning

appeared. The cries of anguish from the 'upper' regions, caused by lack of
additional apprentices and skilled wotkmen recruited for work, became heartrendering.
"They cried with loud voices, 'The fault lies with those workers who confine
their energies to the original temple. We must do something immediately to help
shore up the building lest we perish. Our structure will fall apart and we, being
on top, will sustain the greatest damage.
'Let us aid those poor Brethren down below by pointing out their foolishness

quantity not quality, is needed.
'It is apparent to us that their old, silly ideas of learning the basic skills are
only time-wasting endeavors. We can plainly see that greater numbers are all
that is really necessary, so we must convince these foolish Brethren.
'This is an emergency so hasten, lest our beautiful building goes the way of
all earthly things!!'
"The ideas of the alarmists prevailed, but the changes they accomplished on
the trestleboards had adverse effects. While outside adversaries and the profane
laughed and gloated, the temple collapsed inwardly; and the fall thereof was
very great.''

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, (It is, and can be done.) The chain store industries such as J.
C. Penney, Sears, Roebuck & Company, Montgomery Ward, Kressage, etc. are
self-insured, even to their automobile and liability insurance and are operating
it as a business policy of their own Companies. We can do the same with 400
plus Lodge buildings in the State of California. We can set them up as a cooperative group for a common cause under one operating head. The physicians
and Surgeons have done it, so can we; and
WHEREAS, (Existing insurance is a ripoff.) The records of our Lodge building reveal that it cost $46,000.00 when built. We have spent $48,000 on insurance. The present policy values it at $134,000.00, but because it is not insured for 80% of its replacement value, we could only collect one-half of the
premium price if it burned down . 80% of its replacement value is about
$300,000.00 and Thompkins quoted us $2,000.00 for a one year policy for fire
only. That amount would cost each member of our lodge $12.00 per year for
Fire Insurance only. At the 1977 Grand Lodge Communication, the Insurance
Committee, of which Elmer Gunther is Chairman, reported a $733,000.00 loss
to the 266 Lodges who reported Fire and Casualty insurance over a period of
IO years. $733,000.00 over IO years - $275.50 loss per year per Lodge. Over
that same IO year period, an average of $1,350.00 per year per Lodge for Fire
and Casualty insurance premiums were paid which is 80% above the cost; and
WHEREAS, The Physicians and Surgeons put a bill through the State Legislature to establish a co-operative, non-profit insurance Agreement, which resulted in Section 1.280. 7 being added to the Insurance Code which allows IOOO
individual Physicians and Surgeons to operate under one co-operative head to
self-insure their operations. Their insurance is strictly liability, and the average
premium charged by the Insurance Companies of the 1000 members was
$16,500.00 per year each. Jn the first eleven months of their operation, their
cost per each member's liability was $0.32 plus operational overhead. We cannot
expect that much of a difference, but we can cut our costs for Fire, Vandalism,
and Liability 80% or more; and
WHEREAS, the Grand Lodge Committee on Insurance reported that the Insurance Commissioners office would require the incorporation of a company
classified as reciprocal or interinsurance exchange to be formed; and
WHEREAS, the State Legislature caused section 1280.7 to be added to the
insurance code, which allows the qualification as an unincorporated interindemnity, reciprocal or interinsurance arrangement; and
WHEREAS, the Voters of California on June 6th, 1978 approved a local
agency insurance pooling arrangement, by Legislative Constitutional Amendment to the Constitution.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that we proceed to form our own
Mutual Cooperative Non-Profit Fraternal Lodge Trust Agreement to operate our
own Fire and Casualty Company, under Section 1280. 7 of the Insurance Code;
incorporate if we must, but get on with it because time is wasting and we need
the money that we will save.
Respectfully submitted,
URBAN H. HARTER, M No. 379

Referred to Committees on Policy and General Purposes, Jurisprudence, Finance, Insurance and Temple Properties.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 3 proposes that Grand Lodge form a Mutual Cooperative NonProfit Fraternal Lodge Trust Agreement to operate its own Fire and Casualty
Company, under Section 1280. 7 of the California Insurance Code.
Grand Lodge cannot form a Mutual Cooperative under the above Section
quoted, as it was put into effect only for physicians and surgeons for protection
in the event of suits against them for malpractice liability. Further, a substantial
reserve fund in the order of $700,000 would have to be created by Grand Lodge
for any self-insurance arrangement.
While the particular plan proposed is not feasible, it is appropriate that the
Insurance Committee study ways to keep fire insurance costs as low as possible,
and your Committee on Policy and General Purposes has been advised that the
Insurance Committee is doing that. We should wait for the results of their
studies.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
The Committee on Jurisprudence, to which this Resolution has been referred,
reports as follows:
The Resolution proposes that Grand Lodge form a Mutual Cooperative NonProfit Fraternal Lodge Trust agreement to operate its own Fire and Casualty
company under section 1280. 7 of the Insurance Code of the State of California,
to self-insure Lodge buildings.
Your Committee submits the following:
Incorporation under Section 1280.7 of the Insurance Code is not possible by
Grand Lodge since the provisions of that section are limited to physicians and
surgeons. A non-profit corporation authorized to transact an insurance business
by the Insurance Commissioner of California could be formed. However, sufficient funds to cover the cost of forming and administering the corporation, the
required reserves, and the losses would be required to be deposited and there
would be other prerequisites and required conditions. Under what circumstances
sufficient Temple Associations could, or would, join, whether assessments could
be levied to cover losses, and many other aspects must be known before any
legislation could be drafted. Therefore, your Committee moves that this matter
be referred to an appropriate Committee for study and that the Committee report
to Grand Lodge at the next Annual Communication its finding and proposals.

The Committee on Insurance:
A meeting of the Insurance Committee was held on September 15, 1978 at
1111 California Street, San Francisco for the purpose of discussing Resolution
No. 3, cooperative fire insurance plan which will be presented for consideration
at the Annual Communication October JO, 1978.
The following were present: John R. McKee, Alfred T. Aoyd, Jr., Joseph
Matich, Peter Tripp, Elmer Sandberg, Elmer C. Gunther, Chairman.
Also present: George Frank, Thompkins & Company and Verne Hendrix.
Brother Urban Harter, Worshipful Master of Fillmore Lodge No. 379, the
proponent of Resolution No. 8, was present and Brother Robert Schultz, Estero
Lodge No. 719, Morro Bay was also in attendance.
It was a unanimous recommendation of the committee that Resolution No. 3
should be withdrawn for the following reasons:
I. The Insurance Commissioner for the State of California has advised us that
the Resolution cannot be implemented under Section 1280. 7 of the Insurance Code as is stated in the resolution because that section applies only
to physicians and surgeons and was enacted by the legislature to meet a
specified situation when doctors could not procure liability insurance for
their professional liability.
2. A study by our Insurance Committee over the past two years, after conferring with the Insurance Commissioner's office, has developed that a
self-insurance plan for Temple Associations could be established if all the
Temple properties were under one ownership in which case each Association could be assessed for losses or possibly insured under a blanket policy, but this would require each association to transfer its assets to a holding corporapon or entity to establish single ownership.
3. As an alternative a reciprocal insurance company can be established which
could regulate its own rates according to California law but this would
require an investment of at least $700,000 capital and surplus.

It was therefore recommended that in order to accomplish the intent of Resolution No. 3, which is to possibly reduce the cost of fire and related insurance
covering Temple Association properties through self-insurance or blanket or cooperative plans, that a further study be made and all Temple Associations be
solicited to ascertain if they would be willing to subscribe to either of the two
alternatives stated below:
Transfer their assets to a holding corporation or entity and hold stock or trust
certificates therein.
Help organize a reciprocal insurance company and contribute their share to
a fund of $700,000 necessary capital and surplus.
Therefore, the Insurance Committee recommends a "No" vote on Resolution
No. 3.
The Insurance Committee calls attention to arrangements in effect for some
ti~e past in which Temple Associations may realize substantial savings of premiums for Fire and Liability insurance on their properties through Grand Lodge
facilities, and those Temple Associations who are not already taking advantage
of it should explore this possibility.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, the second paragraph of Section 200 of Article V of the Constitution of the Grand Lodge of California provides for a recommending committee to recommend to the Grand Lodge of California a member of said Grand
Lodge for election as Junior Grand Warden; and
WHEREAS, the third paragraph of said Section 200 provides that each Inspector shall be furnished with the name of said recommendee and his biographical sketch, whereafter each Inspector is required to promptly disseminate by
oral communication and not otherwise, as often as may be necessary, the name
and biographical sketch of said recommendee to the Masters and Wardens of
each Inspectoral District, and through them to other members of Grand Lodge
in their respective Lodges; and
WHEREAS, it is the clear intent of the provisions of said Section 200 that
the Inspectors shall be the instruments which will ensure the election of the
recommendee as Junior Grand Warden; and
WHEREAS, the responsibilities thus placed upon the Inspectors constitute a
sacred trust, violation of which in spirit and in truth should be deemed sufficient
grounds for dismissal from office.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that a new sentence shall be added
to said third paragraph of said Section 200, reading as follows:

"Any failure or neglect on the part of an Inspector to conform to the requirements of this paragraph in spirit and in truth shall constitute sufficient grounds
for his dismissal from office."

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 5 proposes that any failure or neglect upon the part of an
Inspector to conform to the requirements of Section 200 CMC shall constitute
sufficient grounds for dismissal from office. Section 200 CMC prescribes the
manner of election of the officers of the Grand Lodge and includes requirements
for the participation of the Inspectors in disseminating information concerning
the recommendee for the office of Junior Grand Warden .
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes this proposed additional legislation is not needed. Inspectors are appointed annually by the Grand
Master, and it is clearly within the power of the Grand Master to terminate the
service of an Inspector if he should choose to do so. If an Inspector fails to
discharge his duties in accordance with our law, the Grand Master presently has
all the necessary authority to discharge the Inspector if, in his judgment, this
should be done. The discretionary authority of the Grand Master should not be
infringed upon by unnecessary specifics.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.

The Committee on Ritual:
Resolution NQ. 5 proposes that the Inspector, in performing his duties in accordance with Section 200 of Article V of the Constitution of the Grand Lodge
of California, also will see to it that the recommendee for the election as Junior
Grand Warden is elected as the Junior Grand Warden.
In the words of the Brother submitting Resolution No . 5, to quote the third
"whereas," "it is the clear intent of the provisions of said Section 200 that the
Inspector shall be the instrument which will ensure the election of the recommendee as Junior Grand Warden."
The Resolution further goes on to recommend the punishment of an Inspector,
by dismissal from office, for his failure to conform to the requirements of Section
200 in both spirit and truth .
.
As Section 1122 of the California Masonic Code points out, the Inspector is
the representative of the Grand Master in his Distri~t, and we of the Ri~u?~ Committee feel that each Inspector knows well the weight of that responsibibty.
Further the Ritual Committee does not feel that, according to Section 200,
the Inspe~tor shall be the instrument which ensures the election of the Ju?ior
Grand Warden, and to do so would constitute campaigning of the severest kmd.
The Ritual Committee feels that the adoption of this Resolution would serve
no useful purpose in the function of the Grand Lodge, but it would_ put t~e
Inspectors in a position of politicing, which we feel would be degrading their
position and should not be a part of their duties.
We move the adoption of the Resolution, and urge a "No" vote.
Not Adopted.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 6 seeks to amend Section 1050 of the California Masonic
Code. This section is directed to the duty of the Grand Master to preside in the
Grand Lodge at Annual or other communications, and makes him the final authority in his rulings as the presiding officer.
This Resolution would delete the Grand Master's power to be the final authority in his rulings as the presiding officer.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes that to remove this
authority of the Grand Master would completely disrupt and in the long run
lessen the effective democratic debate system we presently enjoy.
The proponent has referred to several Proceedings in our formative years as
a Grand Lodge from 1850 to 1855. A review of the 1852 Proceedings regarding
then Grand Master Hyam deals with his work in making Masons when several
Bay Area Lodges had rejected those men as candidates for the degrees . In other
words , the Grand Master completely ignored the votings of Lodges and overruled the will of the majority.
The Grand Lodge in a Special 1852 Communication to consider this unMasonic conduct, acknowledged that the exalted station had never theretofore
required legislation or regulations to control or cover such a situation. There was
no legislation to try the Grand Master at that time .
Subsequently, this was remedied by what is now Section 3000 of the C.M.C.
The author of the present Resolution in his zeal to subjugate the Grand Master
appears to not consider the effect of Section 3000 of the C.M.C. Under that
Section,:·anytime a Grand Master abuses his duties or powers he may be tried
"for abuse of his power". Therefore, whether it is the Grand Master's duty
under Section 1050 C.M.C . to preside at Communications or attend to other
duties and powers, theFe presently is a means to stop the abuses of a Grand
Master.
Section 1050 relates to the Grand Master's duty to preside at our Communications and "from his rulings as presiding officer there shall be no appeal."

196

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

This Section is not of recent origin; it is found in our 1956 Code as Section 139
and states, "and from his decisions in the chair there shall be no appeal." Earlier
this provision appeared in Ross Digest No. 38-lst.
·
In other words the plain import of Section 1050 is that the Grand Master as
the presiding officer has the final word. This Section just restates the democratic
debate and vote process, Robert's Rules of Order process or any other civilized
process of meetings where someone is chairman, president or the leader. In our
case the Grand Master is our elected leader.
Finally, from a purely practical standpoint, this Resolution makes no provision
for who shall make the final rulings when the Grand Master presides should this
Resolution be adopted. This would create chaos with no person or entity to make
rulings.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes strongly recommends a
"No" vote.

OFFICERS' ASSOCIATIONS-ATTENDANCE
VOLUNTARY
(8)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS, Masonry in California and Hawaii, during the last twenty-five
years has passed in a uniformly straight line descent from an annual NET
GROWTH RATE of more than six thousand members per year to an annual NET
LOSS RATE of three thousand five hundred per year in a State which is growing
by leaps and bounds; and
WHEREAS, this retrogression is readily traceable to the type of leadership,
regimentation and strait-jacket thinking being taught in the Officers' Associations by the District Inspectors under the guise of supervising the meetings of
the Associations, "for the purpose of instruction in those portions of the Constitution and Regulations which relate to the government of the Lodge, for instruction in the proper administration of the affairs of the Lodges and such other
matters as may be for the welfare of the Craft"; and
WHEREAS, this type of instruction which covers the whole field of Lodge
administration, in effect, circumvents the right of a Master to govern his Lodge

WILSON 0. WADE, PM No. 328

Referred to Committees on Policy and General Purposes, Jurisprudence and
on Ritual.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 8 proposes to change paragraph 3rd of Section 1122, C.M.C .
This resolution, if adopted, would make attendance at District Officers' Association meetings voluntary.
It is not always possible for all officers to attend all meetings of Officers'
Associations, and the existing law does permit officers to be excused for due
cause. However, relaxing the mandatory rule is not the answer to the "ills" the
proponent contends are present in our Lodges.
The purpose of Officers or District Association meetings is for consideration
of both ritual and administrative activities. This is a vital function of such meetings and the vehicle by which Grand Lodge and the individual Lodges and officers communicate.
The meetings under consideration in no way usurp the authority of the Master
of a Lodge. These meetings help the officers to govern . They offer a forum for
an exchange of ideas as well as a means of communicating information to the
Lodges.
We recommend no change in our law as to mandatory attendance at meetings
of the Officers' Associations and, accordingly, your Committee on Policy and
General Purposes recommends a "No" vote.

200

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

The Committee on Jurisprudence:
The Committee on Jurisprudence indicated that the language of the Resolution
was adequate and moved its adoption.
The Committee on Ritual:
Resolution No. 8 would lead us to believe that Masonry is a police-state
Fraternity whose basic tenets are those of compulsory indoctrination, regimentation, uniformity and subjugation. It would also have us believe that becoming
familiar with the rules and regulations of Freemasonry, as found in the California
Masonic Code, removes the rights of the Master of a Lodge to rule and govern
his Lodge.
My Brethren, nothing could be further from the truth than what I have just
stated. All of us sitting in this Grand Lodge have attended meetings of an Officers' Association, and in reflection I am sure you will all agree that the function
of the Officers' Association is as stated in Section 1122, 3rd," ... for the purpose
of instruction in those portions of the Constitution and Regulations of the Grand
Lodge which relate to the government of the Lodge ... "
Remember, if you will, that the Inspectors are there always to aid and assist,
to help define a question regarding the Code, to support the officers, coaches
and Masters, and to guide the officers of the Lodges in their Districts in such
a manner that they do not find themselves in conflict with the Code.
Yes, Section 1122, 3rd, of the C.M.C. states that it is the duty of the officers
in the Inspector's District to attend the Officers' Association meetings, and that
failure to do so without due cause or excuse could result in grounds for removal
from office. But, in checking the attendance rosters of the Districts in a Division
in Northern California, and one in Southern California, we find that although
the attendance at these meetings has been less than 100%, the Inspectors have
displayed true Masonic compassion in the discharge of their duties, as related
to the Masonic Code. Is this regimentation? Is this compulsory indoctrination?
On the contrary, Brethren, this is Masonry in action.
Ours is a benevolent Fraternity teaching Brotherly Love, Relief and Truth,
and we of the Ritual Committee submit to you that the Inspectors do teach, but
also are acting in full accordance with the responsibility they have as the
representatives of the Grand Master.
We therefore recommend the adoption of this resolution, but urge a "No"
vote.
Not Adopted.
