The Committee O'} Policy and General Purposes:
The Grand Master in 1967 and again in 1968 recommended that a study be
made of the question of reimbursement of members of Grand Lodge for expenses
incurred in attending to their duties.
A special Finance Study Committee, chaired by PGM Herbert Huebner, (then
Senior Grand Warden), reported its recommendations at the 1969 Communication, and those recommendations were adopted as the law of the Grand Lodge.
In researching the question of Inspectors' travel and other expenses incurred
at Annual Communications, the special Finance Study Committee of 1969
learned of numerous inequities as to moneys provided to Inspectors for attending
Grand Lodge. Some Inspectors received no funds from any source to defray
their expenses while other Inspectors were given quite large sums. The sources
of these funds were usually Lodges, some donating directly to the Inspector and
others donating through Officers' Associations. In some instances funds were
provided by an Officers' Association whose source of funds was not always
clearly defined.
At any rate the Committee learned that some Lodges resented having to make
such donations. Also, in some areas a spirit of competition seemed to have developed as to which Association or Lodge could provide their Inspector with the
best "plum." Some Lodges were hard pressed for operating funds and so could
not spare extra money for an Inspector's expenses. In all fairness, however, we
should know that many of the Inspectors who received gratuities used a sizeable

204

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

portion of those funds to provide refreshments for members of their Districts
All in all; however, it was a cloudy situation and fundamentally unfair becaus~
not all Inspectors received equal treatment or compensation.
The 1969 law adopted by the Grand Lodge provided equitable reimbursement
for all Inspectors and also prohibited any payment to them by Lodges or District
Officers' Associations.
In arriving at its decision to include Inspectors in an expense reimbursement
plan, t~e 1969 S~cial Stud~ Committee determined that, although no regular
or special duty might be assigned to Inspectors at Annual Communications of
th~ ~rand Lodge, still in all an Inspector (representing the Grand Master in his
D1stnct) could be and wa.s a leader to the Lodge officers of his District, many
of whom. would ~e attending Grand Lodge for the first time. Thus the Inspector
could guide and· instruct all these officers in the affairs of the Annual Communication.
Also, at that time, Inspectors were required to attend the Grand Lecturer's
annual School of Instruction held just prior to the Annual Communication.
While a succeeding Grand Lecturer has discontinued that School of Instruction, and while the reported activities of some Inspectors at last year's Annual
Communication might be construed as not in accord with our Masonic Law
your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes that an Inspector'~
~res.ence at Grand Lodge is valuable to Lodge officer- delegates and to the functioning of Grand Lodge. We also have learned that progressive Elective Grand
~dge ?fficers ma~ ask Inspectors to attend a planning meeting or other meetings pnor to or dunng the Annual Communication.
We ~onc~ude, therefore, the present system of reimbursement is proper and
we believe it should be continued.
I move the adoption of Resolution No . 10 and your Committee on Policy and
General Purposes urges a "No" vote.

this resolution to codify Annotation 2042b, and which would also include codification of Annotation 2646b, is proper.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "Yes" vote.
The Commitlee on Jurisprudence:
The Committee on Jurisprudence, to which this Resolution was referred, reports as follows:
This Resolution proposes an amendment to Section 2042 of the California
Masonic Code to make it mandatory for the Master of a Lodge to direct that the
Tiler, if a member of the Lodge, be relieved of his duties as Tiler so that he may
vote on questions before the Lodge and balloting · on applications, if the Tiler
requests it.

The Committee on Ritual:
Section 2646 of the California Masonic Code states "That every member of
a Lodge, when present, must vote upon a ballot for degrees or for affiliation."
The last paragraph of this section states that "The 'Lodge Room' does not
include the Tiler's room or preparation room."
Section 2034b of the CMC states that "The Tiler is present at a Lodge meeting, even though he is not in the Lodge Room, but is at his post in the Tiler's
room ."
Section 2646b of the CMC states that "The Tiler should be granted the privilege of debating and voting on questions before the Lodge, if a member, and
should be relieved of his duties for the purpose ."
We of the Committee on Ritual are of the opinion that the above noted sections
of the Masonic Code serve the intent and purpose of Resolution No. 12.
We move the adoption of the resolution and urge a "No" vote.
The Resolution received a simple majority vote. Failing a 5/6 affirmative vote,
the matter will be held over until the 1979 Annual Communication.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 14 proposes to amend Section 2124, Paragraph 12, C.M.C.
to permit Research Lodges to vote upon applications for membership at the
Stated Meeting at which they are submitted and read.
This proposal was contained in Resolution No. 15 presented at the 1977 Annual Communication, to amend Section 2124 C.M.C. to permit Research Lodges
to receive applications for membership without the requirement of referral to a
Committee of three for investigation and a report thereon.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes was in favor of that portion
of the Resolution. However, it also included the proposal of Resolution No. 14
to permit Research Lodges to vote upon applications for membership at the same
Stated Meeting at which they were submitted and read. Your Committee was
opposed to that portion of the Resolution and the proponent consented to delete
it. This was done and the Resolution was then adopted as amended.
It is the opinion of your Committee on Policy and General Purposes that NO
application for membership in ANY Lodge in this Jurisdiction should be voted
upon at the same Stated Meeting at which it is submitted and read, but should
be voted upon at the next Stated Meeting following its receipt.
This Resolution proposes a complete departure of established procedure and
has very serious implications of precedence which should not be permitted.
It is the unanimous opinion of your Committee that there should be NO deviation from the established procedure for election to membership in the Jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California and strongly recommend a "No" vote.

Respectfully submitted,
HERBERT M. McCRACKEN' PM No. 560
Referred to Committees on Policy and General Purposes and Jurisprudence.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Resolution No. 15 proposes that plural membership be prohibited when such
plural membership is in Lodges within the same Inspectoral District. The preamble to this proposed Resolution indicates that there can be conflict of interest in
such plural membership situations because of proximity of one Lodge to the
other.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes fails to find any substantial
reason for this proposal. Close proximity of one Lodge to another is certainly
a fact in urban areas, but there are also areas where the Lodges composing an
Inspectoral District are many miles apart. If the conduct of a plural member is
such that it is deemed harmful to one of the Lodges of which he is a member,
surely good counsel with that member by Officers of the Lodge should in most
instances alleviate any problem. If the offending member's conduct is un-Masonic in nature, the California Masonic Code provides avenues for disciplinary
action.
Again, your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes there is no
need for the proposed legislation and recommends a "No" vote.
The Committee on Jurisprudence:
The Committee on Jurisprudence to which Resolution No. 15 entitled "Multiple Membership-Within Same Inspectoral Districts" was referred reports as
follows:
Since the legislation proposed by the proponent of this Resolution did not
cover the situation of dual members, that is, those ·who belong to Lodges of
other Grand Jurisdictions which allow dual membership and who reside in this
Jurisdiction and affiliate with a Lodge of this Grand Lodge, but it appears from
the Resolution that this was the intention of the proponent, your Committee
wrote to the proponent to clarify this question, and have been assured that the
proponent intends to cover both situations.

To The Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:

form. This may also tend to bring more members into the fold.

with Masonic Honors," be changed to read, " but may be burie.d with Masonic

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS , Masonry is a universal Fraternity of Brothers; and
WHEREAS , Masonic ritual throughout the worlJ is basically the same, with
only nuances of differences from one Jurisdiction to another; and
WHEREAS, California attracts many Past Masters from throughout the world,
whether for employment or in retirement; and
WHEREAS, these Past Mas ters individually and collectively provide a tremendous reservoir of talents and abilities; and
WHEREAS, these talents and abilities are inclined to lie fallow in California
under our present regulations; and
WHEREAS, it would accrue to the benefit of Masonry in our great Jurisdiction
to be able to call upon these talents.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that appropriate Sections of the
California Masonic code-namely Section 2540, et al-be amended so as to
allow a Past Master of a duly recognized Lodge from without our Juri sdiction
to become a member of the Grand Lodge of California, provided:
I. That said Past Master has properly affiliated with a Lodge of thi s Jurisdiction and is, thereafter, recommended for membership in California
GranJ Lodge by the Master and Wardens of the Lodge of our Jurisdiction
with which he has affiliated. and then ,
2. That said Past Master has proven his familiarity with the ritual of this
Jurisdiction by successful completion of a proficiency examination as devised by the Grand Lodge Ritual Committee; and
3. That said Past Master has proven his knowledge of California Masonry by
successful completion of a wrinen examination similar to that required of
Masters-elect of California Lodges; and

BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that the appropriate Grand Lodge Committee(s)- be it the Committee on Ritual and/or others- as designated by the Grand
Mas ter, be charged with establishing and publishing proper criteria to carry out
the intent of this Resolution so that Past Mas ters , as defined herein, may have
the opportunity of qualifying themselves to become members of this Grand
Lodge prior to the 1979 Annual Communication of the Most Worshipful Grand
Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of the State of California.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This Resolution would permit Masons who have been Masters of Lodges in
other duly recognized Jurisdictions to become members of this Grand Lodge
under certain circumstances.
The basic policy question is the principle. Shall this Grand Lodge allow as
membeers under any circumstances Past Masters from o ther Grand Juri sdictions?
This proposal would dilute the prestige of Past Masters of this Jurisdiction.
Further, Constituent Lodges need the leadership which can be provided by Past
Masters of other Jurisdictions. Such a Brother can become a leader in a Lodge
in this Jurisdiction and when he has been a Master here he will become a memher
of this Grand Lodge. This is our policy and it should be preserved.
The Policy and General Purposes Committee recommends a "No" vote.

The Commiuee on Jurisprudence:
The Committee on Jurisprudence. to which this Resolution has been referred,
reports as follows:
The proponents of Resolution No. 18 seek to amend the California Masonic
Code to permit a Past Master from a Lodge in a Grand Jurisdiction recognized
by the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of California to become a
member of this Grand Lodge.
The proponents give the following reasons and purposes for this Resolutio n:
I. Masonry is a universal Fraternity of Brother .
2 . Masonic ritual throughout the world is basicall y the same with only nuances from one Jurisdiction to another.
3. Whether by reason of their employment or their retirement, many Past
Masters from throughout the world live in California .
4 . These Past Masters individually and collectively arc a tremendous reservoir
of talent and ability . Under our present regulatio ns, their talents and abilities tend to be unused . It would benefit Masonry in California to be able
to call upon the talents and abilities of these Past Masters .
To carry out the intent of the proponents , your Committee submits the following legislation:
RESOL YEO, that Section 2540 be amended by adding at the end of the first
paragraph the following sentence :
"Such Past Master of a Lodge within the jurisdiction of another Grand Lodge
may become a member of this Grand Lodge as a Past Master of the Lodge
with which he is affiliated if he passes to the satisfaction of the Ritual Committee an examination as prepared by it in the Ritual of this Jurisdiction and
a written examination is prepared by it similar to the examination in Jaw and
procedure then required of Masters-elect of thi s Jurisdiction, and if he has
also been recommended in writing for membership in this Grand Lodge by
the Master and Wardens of the Lodge in this Jurisdiction with which such
Past Master is affiliated."

The Committee on Ritual:
Legislation of this type makes us, as individuals, wonder if it was not designed
for one certain individual or. possibly , a mino r few . Past Masters of other Jurisdictions are most welcome to affiliate with our Lodges, go through the chairs
and beco me members of our Grand Lodge in the same manner that each of has
done . Our Lodges could most certainly use them .
We , as a Committee, have no argument with the intent of the Resolution ,
providing it serves a useful purpose . The proponents of this Resolution are to
be commended for recognizing that there is talent available in Past Masters from
other Jurisdictions. This talent could be most useful at the Lodge level and,
when qualified, at the Grand Lodge level.
Brethren. this Grand Lodge is yours; you ma ke the laws and uphold those
Jaws. We of the Ritual C ommittee are willing to implement a test ritual and a
written examination. if called upon to do so.
Your Committee on Ritual moves the adoption of the resolution and make~
no recommendation.
Not Adopted.

Our ancient Brethren were, most probably, concerne d that the physically handicapped would be a detriment to the Fraternity , for they could not be bearers of
burden or hewers in the quarries and not having done e ither of the above, most
definitely , could not bec ome overseers of the work. This was o perative Masonry
at work. We are speculative Masons. The physically handicapp ed would not and
should not be a burden to our Fraternity in today's society .
Resolutio ns in the past have had minor defects, such as Resolution No. 17
in 1976 which was a 1977 carryover proposal and failed by less than 5 votes.
Your Committe e, at th at time, conceded that the legislation was not the perfect
instrumen t , but with patience and perserver ance, it could become a means of
great good for our Fraternity . The only defect your Co mmittee could find in that
legislatio n was the section that stated, "Where necessary , another Brother who
is qualified to d o so may at the request of the Maste r act as a proxy for the
candidate . " This line has been removed from Resolutio n No. 19. Removal of
this line will cause the candidate to participate for himself.

pose is the revision of the similiarly numbered Resolution No. 20, concerning
amendment of application forms for degrees and for affiliation. adopted at the
Annual Communication of 1977, reported at pages 249 and 250 of the 1977
Proceedings.
By means of la~t year's Resolution No. 20, the Grand Lodge took recognition
of the impact of the Fair Credit Reporting Act adopted by the Congress of the
United States, and related Jaws and regulations, upon Lodge investigations of
applicants for the degrees and for affiliation; and, to facilitate compliance therewith , authorized addenda deemed appropriate at the time to the applications for
the degrees and for affiliation.
The stated purpose of the Federal Fair Credit Reporting Act is to require that
consumer reporting agencies adopt reasonable procedures for meeting the needs
of commerce for consumer credit, perso nnel , insurance and other information
in a manner that is fair and equitable to the consumer. with regard to the confidentiality, accuracy, relevancy, and proper utilization of ~uch information in
accordance with the requirements of the Federal Fair Credit Reporting Act. Provision is made in the Act for extensive rules, regulations and procedures in the
preparation. content and use o f consumer reports, including pre ~cribed remedies,
penalties and fines for noncompliance . Under the Act, a consumer reporting
agency may furni sh a consumer report only under certain enumerated circumstances, one being in accordance with the written instruction ~ of the consumer
to whom it relates.
Since many Lodges obtain consumer reports from consumer reporting agencies when investigating applicants for the degrees and affiliation, it is imperative
that adequate written consent and instructions be furnished by every applicant
for the protectio n of the Lodges under the Act.
The California 'Consumer Credit Reporting Agencies Act and the California
Investigative Consumer Reporting Agencies Act, at the state level. build upon
the Federal Fair Credit Reporting Act, having many of its provisions and in other
respects going beyond those of the Federal Fair Credit Reporting Act. Thus ,
under the California laws, adequate written consent and instructions from th~
applicant become even more important to us in the conduct of investigations.
To our knowledge. the State of Hawaii has not as yet enacted a comparable
statute of its own, but our Constituent Lodges in Hawaii are, of course, governed
by the Federal Fair Credit Reporting Act, which applies to every state in the
nation.
In the opinion of your Committee on Jurisprudence, the legislation adopted
as Resolution No. 20 in 1977 is insufficient to afford the fullest mea ure of
protection needed under these laws and should be revised at this I 978 Communication of the Grand Lodge to require more expansive and detailed written
consent and instructions from applicants for the degrees and for affiliation, together with as complete a release from liability from applicants as possi ble.
Our Chairman. as proponent. has incorporated in this year's Resolution No.
20 all of the essential factors for the best possible revision of last year's Resolution No. 20 to meet the requirements of the law~ re ferred to, including a much
improved and more implicit form of written consent and instructions by applicants for inclusion in applications for the degrees and for affiliation along with
a more comprehensive hold harmless and release clause.

ONE YEAR WAITING PERIOD-DELETE
(21)
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
WHEREAS. the requirement for a newly rai sed Mason to wait one year before
petitioning a concordant body adopted by this Grand Lodge has shown no beneficial results; and
WHEREAS , thirty-three Jurisdictions require no waiting period. including
several wbich have enjoyed long and continued inc rease in membership; and
WHEREAS . attendance at any and all Masonic or affiliated meetings should
be e ncouraged since our attendance figures continue to decline; and
WHEREAS. California is one of the seventee n Jurisdicti ons which has
adopted no minimum waiting period between Degrees; therefore, it seems that
a delay of twelve months to petition an affiliated body is excessive; and
WHEREAS. California is one of only seven out of sixty-five Grand Lodges,
listed in the List of Lodges, which require a wait of twel ve months.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that that portion of Section 2635
regarding the one year waiting period be deleted, and that Question 15 of the
Application for Degrees Form be revised to exc lude this requirement.
Respectfully submitted,

It may wel I be asked- has it acco mplished the intended purpose?
The argument that affiliation with the Scott ish Rite, York Rite and Shrine will
preempt a Brother' s time to devote to his Lodge is questiona ble. T his is demonstrated by the large number of Masons who have many Masoni c affiliations,
yet are active in the affairs of their Lodges . Many have become acti ve in their
Lodges only a fter the fla me was kind led by activity in an affiliated organization.

the one year waiti ng period would benefit only the Concordant Bodies is also
questionable.
Your Committee points out the fact that this Resolution does not affect the
requirement that a Master Mason must demonstrate his proficiency in the Candidate's Lecture of the Third Degree before he may join prerequisite bodies .

the proficiency requirement.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This Reso lut ion requires of a Candidate the proficiency in the Master Mason
Degree prior to sig ning the By-Laws and becoming a member of the Lodge.
The adoption of this Resolution wo uld create a new class of Mason who has
received the Th ird Degree but is denied the rights and privileges of a Master
Mason for an indefin ite period . The Candidate could be prevented fro m taking
hi s proficiency fo r reasons beyond his control. Should he d ie during that interval
he could not receive a Masonic buri al nor would his family have the rights and
benefit~ which the ritual of the T hird Degree indicates to be their due . During
the period between receiving the Master Mason Degree and the completion of
the proficiency our Brother would be in the position of a Master Mason unaffiliated and unrecognized becau se he had been den ied. perhaps by circumstances
be yond hi s co ntrol, fro m complying with the requirements for signing the ByLaws of his Lodge.
Your Committee believes in the importance of the proficiency in the Thi rd
Degree . but feels this can best be emphasized by impressing upon the Candidate
his responsibility and not by creating two classe~ of Master Masons.

The Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This Resolution proposes to authorize the use of a cipher or code ritua l by the

Officers and Officer's Coaches. The ritual is to be published by the Grand Lodge
of California.
There is no evidence that those Grand Juri sdictions which sanction the use of
cipher rituals do better in communicating the ritual of the three degrees. On the
contrary, the reputation of the Grand Lodge of California for outstanding conferral of our ritual is widely recognized. Your Committee further concurs in the
report of the Jurisprudence Committee of seventy years ago which stated:
l. Freemasonry has as essentials cenain secrets of ritual which it forever conceals and never reveals to any person except its own memhers .
2. These ancient my ste ries are communicated only by the instructive tongue
to the attentive ear and are safely lodged in the faithful breast and any
other mode of communication in Craft Masonry is forbidden in solemn
form and manner.
3. So, likewise, is forbidden the writing, printing. marking in any manner
of these secrets or any sign or letter thereof whereby the same becomes
legible or intelligible to any person, lest these secrets might become known
to the profane .
4 . No individual Mason is exempt from the obligation of profound secrecy .
5. Truly these secrets are ancient landmarks of Freemasonry.
Standing upon these ancient precepts of our Brotherhood, we are not at liberty
to violate them nor to encourage or sanction their violation by others of our
Fraternity .
In the spirit of preserving that which is good and beneficial in our ancient
heritage, your Committee on Policy and General Purposes recommends a "No"
vote.

The Committee 011 Ritual:
Resolution No. 23 proposes to have published a cipher ritual or approve the
use of an existing cipher ritual.
The proponents of Resolution No. 23 state that cipher rituals are permitted
in Hawaii .
Hawaii is under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California and cipher
rituals are not permitted in our Jurisdicti on.
The Ritual Committee does not condone the use of cipher rituals and feel very
strongly that any violation of our Code should be reported so that proper action
may be taken .
We would also point out that it is against our law for any sojourner living
under our Jurisdiction to use a cipher ritual.
In Jurisdictions where cipher rituals are permitted it has not helped attendance;
attendance ha~ declined and we find the cipher ritual being used in open Lodge
and that it has not helped the Officers to be more proficient in their work .
The ritual problem in many of our Lodges is with the written part, the monitorial and not the esoteric work.
The ritual in the Jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California has withstood
the test of time and is the envy of all other Jurisdictions . The Resolution if passed
would be contrary to our obligations as Masons.
We move the Resolution be adopted and recommend a "No" vote.
A simple majority voted for the Resolution . Failing the 5/6 affirmative vote
for passage , the Re sol ut ion will be held over until the 1979 Annual
Communication.

VOTE REQUIRED-PR OPOSED AMENDMENTS

(28)
To rhe Mosr Worshipful Grand lodge. F. & A. M . of California:
WHEREAS. it is extremely difficult to pass or amend any ordinances under
the present requirement of five-sixths of the votes of the Annual Communication;
and
WHEREAS, many financial, morale and practical detriments result from proposed amendments lying over for one year.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE JT RESOLVED that Section 4002 of the C . M.C.
be amended to substitute two-thirds for five-sixths; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED that Section 4004 of the C.M.C. be deleted.
Respectfully submitted,
HOWARD J. CONDON, PM No.296

WAYNER. LEE, PM No.296

Referred to Committees o n Policy and General Purposes and Jurisprudence.

The Commitree on Policy and General Purposes:
Our present ordinances provide that if a proposed amendment receives more
than a majority vote but less than the 5/6 required for its adoption it shall be
held over for one year to the next Annual Communication at which time a 2/ 3
vote shall be sufficient for its adoption.
The proposed Resolution No. 28 would reduce the required vote on the proposed resolution to 2/J and delete the provision for carry over.
Our present regulations have proven effective for 100 years. More than 100
years ago a unanimous ballot was required the first year , but a majority vote
caused the matter to be carried over for one year when it was passed if it rece ived
a 2/J vote. (See Proceedings of 1861.)
The 5/6 a nd 2/3 vote req uirement provde a desirable stab ility in our M asonic
law and has not prevented the passage of sound and reasonable legislation in the
past.
The proposed change reducing the re4uired vote to 2/J could permit too easy
and too speedy passage of needless and unnecessary changes in our procedure .
As a matter of policy therefore your Committee on Policy and General Purposes is opposed to this change and recommends a "No" vote .
The Commirree on Jurisprudence:
The Committee on Jurisprudence reponed that the language of the Resolution
was ade4uate to carry out the intent of the proponents and moved its adopt ion.
Not Adopted.

REPORT 9F CALIFORNIA MASONIC FOUNDATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand l odge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Board of Trustees of the California Masonic Foundation has endeavored
to carry out the mandate of this Grand Lodge. as expressed in Section 1602 et
seq of the California Masonic Code.
To accomplish those purposes we have, during the fiscal year July I. 1977-June
30, 1978, approved 60 scholarship awards to needy and worthy students in a
total sum of $36,400.00. Of these, 26 totaling $ 15,600.00 were granted from
funds made available by the Order of the Amaranth, as provided in the Trust
Agreement between that O rder and our Foundation.
During that same period, grants in a total sum of $ 10,000.00 were made to
the Northern and Southern Juri sdiction s of the Order of DeMolay, Grand Bethel
of Job's Daughters, and O rder of Rain bow fo r Girls. for education al purposes
in connec tion with their leadership training programs.
Grants of $5,000.00 each were made to the Crippled Children's Societies of
Los Angeles and Santa Clara Counties, for maintenance of summer camps for
handicapped pe rsons in Cali fo rnia. Interplast Plastic Reconstruction Surgery at
Stanford Hospital received a grant in the sum of $5,000.00 fo r charitable medical
and scientific purposes.
The Investments, Income and Expenses of the Foundation are set fort h in the
repon of the Grand Treasurer and the financial statements of the Auditor's reports and are there fore not repeated herein.

REPORT OF
LODGE RESOURCES DEVELOPMENT COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grnnd lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The second year of existence of the Lodge Resources Development Committee
has been an enjoyable and an eventful one.
It is the unique charge of this Committee to pay attention to those problems
which beset our Lodges generally. The commonest complaints are loss of members, poor attendance at meetings and lack of suitable officer material.
When Lodges decide that something must be done in one or more of these
fields, they usually talk to the Inspector and with his assistance, a report is made
to the Grand Master. He then determines whether it is a case which should be
referred to the Committee. When authorized by the Grand Master, the Committee contacts the Lodge and arranges for a meeting.
Several Lodges have been helped in this manner during the year. The identity
of the Lodges is known to the Grand Master but will not be set forth in this
printed report.
The Committee held two organizational and planning sessions, one in Los
Angeles and one in Oakland. The meetings were of great help to the Committee
and we recommend they be continued. Committee members living in Northern
California attend the meeting in Oakland. Members in Southern California attend
the Los Angeles meeting.
Printed helps have been developed for the assistance of Lodges. One is entitled
"Keeping Masonry on the Move". The other is "12 Questions on Freemasonry". We recommend that these be kept in stock by the Grand Lodge Supply
Room.
Near the mid-point of the year, a new and important assignment was given
the Committee. It relates to "Laymen's Nights" . Programs intended to reach
non-Masons have developed during the last few years. An incidental purpose
is in educating our own members concerning what they can and should tell others
about Freemasonry.
These programs grew on a "hit and miss" basis without organized control.
Some were excellent and some were not so good.
It becan1e evident to rhc Grand Master that organization wa s necessary. There
was a real need for well-prepared speakers.
At this point, the. project was assigned to the Lodge Resources Development
Committee. The Committee organized two training sessions, one at Los Angeles
and one in San Francisco. Speakers approved by the Grand Master were invited .
'Thirty men residing in Southern California attended the Los Angeles session.

Respectfully submitted,

w. BLAIR RIXON

REPORT OF INVESTMENT COMMITTEE
FOR FISCAL. YEAR ENDING J UN E JO,

1978

To the Most Worshipful Grand l odge, F. & A. M. of Californiu:
The Investment Committee repo rts activities for the fiscal year ended June 30,
1978 .
Equity prices in July. 1977 continued to de teriorate as had been the experience
since mid-1976. Generally, this rnndition was brought about by a sharp decline
in th e value of the U.S. do llar in international trade. persistent inflation and
unemploy ment , and expansion of the money supply through the permissive ac-

24.5

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALI FOR!'IA

tivities of the Federal Reserve Board and deficit spending by the Federal Government. In the first quarter of calendar 1978. share prices began to move upward
as domestic corporations took advantage of a cheaper U.S . dollar abroad to raise
prices and improve profitability. Consumer spending remained strong . gi ven
significant support through ever growing gove rnment transfer payments (increased allowances to benefic iaries of social security. we lfare and related pro·
grams). Consumer debt continues to rise at an almost alarming rate. While the
economy generally appears healthy . the quality of its strength appears to be de·
teriorating. Fixed-income securit ies have continued to decline in value, which
offer significantly higher current yields. Mo reover . the spread or difference in
yield between highest quality securities and those with less favorable characteristics is and continues very narrow. Our advisor. Alliance Capital Management
Corporation. continues to favor extending average maturity , investment in direct
U.S. Treasury obligatio ns and other AAA rated debt securities . Further. in antic ipation of higher interest rates later in calendar 1978. Alliance recommended
maintaining a relatively short average maturity. which is now in the process of
being extended in order to maintain the relatively attractive current yields available and the purchase of discount obligations to protect against early call in the
event that interest rates dee line in the future .
The consolidated portfolios of the Grand l odge have the following charac·
teri stics as of June 30, 1978. The fixed-income sector is 5217r invested in AAA
rated obligations. up from 38%1 a year ago . Average maturity is 14.05 years as
compared with 15.32 years on June 30, 1977 . Weighted quality has a numerkal
rating of 3.74 versus 3.41 a year ago. Straight debt iss ues represent 48 .8% of
the total value . versus 42.3'k a year ago.
Convertible securities currently represent 9 .317r of the total value as compared
wi th 12.1 'k a year ago. The rally in share prices has made these securities l es~
anractive and the Investment Committee has authorized sale of a number of
issues.
Just prior to the end of the fi scal year. equity holdings have been modestly
reduced . Representing 48 . 1% of value at the fi scal year end, this compared with
45 .6% a year ago.
Reflecting both a decline in market value for debt and equity issues together
with withdrawals to finance construction of Masonic Home facilities for o ur
members. the June 30. 1978 value of the consolidated po rtfolios was $56. l
million as compared with $62. 1 million as of June 30. 1977 . Estimated annual
income for the year ahead stands at $3 . 96 mill ion for a current yield of 7. ICk
and compares quite favorabl y with the June 30. 1977 estimated annual income
of $3.89 m illio n and a current yield on market of 6.3%.
Ynur Investment Committee continues to be guided by the restrictions of our
Masonic Code and written investment policy adopted and periodically revised .
In addition, the Committee serves as an advisor to the Masonic Retirement Plan
with fiduciary responsibility resting with an independent board of trustees .
It is the stated policy of your Committee to generate max imum income within
a conservative policy which permits less than no rn1al risk . Thus, the portfo lio
tends to decline less than the market averages in a falling market and appreciate
less in market rallies . You should be aware that inflationary pressures act agai nst
the long-term capabilities of our funds since the dollars of income generated buy

less and less each year. Thus. it is essential that we continue to strive to obtain
gifts and bequests for the current and future benefit of o ur members.

REPORT OF RETIREMENT PENSION
PLAN COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M . of California:

Subsequent to the approval by Grand Lodge of a retirement income plan fo r
its employees, the Masonic Homes of California was the first of our several
ent ities to adopt such a plan-to be effective January I, 1955 . Employees of the
Grand Lodge of California. through action o n the part of the Grand Lodge. became participants in the Pl an effective January I , 1956 and employees of com·
poncnt organi zations of the Grand Lodge became participants effective December 8, 1958. And it is safe to say that the existence of a retirement plan for those
who have served. and for those who are now serving us in many capacities . has
contributed materially to the successes which the Masonic Fraternity in Cali·
fo rnia has enjoyed .
Revisions to the o riginal Plan were made during subsequent years to provide
improvements in employee panicipation and benefits; and the Plan was last
amended and restated effective January 1, 1976 to place the Plan in full compliance with requirements of the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of
1974. commonly referred to as ERISA. The Plan is now known as the California
Masonic Retirement Plan.
Our report last year called attention to legislation affecting the operation of
the Pl an adopted by Grand l odge at the l976 Annual Communication. Additional operating changes afforded by the new legislation and regulations have
been made in our administrtive and investment procedures . These changes have
resulted in a smoother and more efficient administration of the Plan.
The Committee has reviewed the annual repo rt for the year ended December
31, 1977 prepared by our actuaries, Coates and Crawford, financial statement
prepared by the Grand Lodge accounting staff, the annual audit repon prepared
by our public accountants and statements prepared by our investment counselor
and by the Trustee for the Plan , Wells Fargo Bank .
The summary of investments at cost held by the Plan as of December JI ,
1977, not including accruals for income and expenses, was $1,980,516 compared to S 1,880.176 for the year ended December 31. 1976. Market value of
investments December 31, 1977 was $1 ,594,774 . The difference of $385,742
between cost and market represents 19.48%. a slightly higher percentage than

247

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

the comparable figure for the preceding year. However. the actuarial value of
:issets a~ of Decembe r 31, 1977. determined to satisfy the requirements of
ERlSA. was $1.773,149, arrived at by using cost value ofbomJs in the portfolio
and a three year moving average on a market value hasis (1975. 1976 and 1977)
for equities.
Net investment income (including accruals) as determined by the actuaries for
purposes of their schedules was $101,718 after allowing $8.018 for net capital
loss on the sale of two securities and $17.591 for Trustees' fees. act uarial services, auditors· fees. investment counseling. office expenses and insurance fees.
Net investment income for the year showed a gain of $19,699 over the preceding
year.
As noted in the report of the Committee last year. again, there has been no
significant change thi s year in the number of active participants in the Plan, both
as to the Masonic Homes of California and the Grand Lodge of California and
its component organizations. The same holds true for non-active. o r retired participants. However, with increasing payroll s and longer spans of employment.
retire ment benefits to be paid to retirees in the future will. no doubt. increase.
The number of retired participating employees from the Masonic Homes of
California increased last year from 43 to 49, and retirement benefits for the year
ended December 31, 1977 increased from $36.683 to $43,558 . For the Grand
Lodge and its component organizations, the number of retired particirants increased by one from 19 to 20 and the reti rement benefits paid increased fro m
$25. 194 to $26 .466.
We reported last year o n several new assumptions used by the actuaries in the
determination of the employer contribution rates. including the use of a 5% return o n invested funds. The assumption that invested funds will continue to earn
59<' annually has been continued in the calculations for this year. The e mployer
contribution rates to be paid this year have been determined by the actuaries
usi ng data taken from the report of the Trustee, Wells Fargo Bank, the report
being that for the year ended December 3 l, 1977. Needless to say, as does the
cost of everything with which we arc confronted increase constantly. so has the
cost of maintaining our retirement plan for the benefit of those who serve us in
various capacities.
The recommended employer contribution rate thi s year for the Masonic
Homes of California is 5. 97<Jc- as opposed to 5.529" last year. The reco mmended
employer contribution rate for the Grand Lodge and its component organizations
is 12.34<Jc- as opposed to 11.21 % last year.
At December 31, 1976. the Plan held slightly in excess of $90,000 in U.S.A.
Treasury and Federal obligat io ns. As of December 31, 1977, the Plan held
$216.500 in similar obligations. As of the close of the Grand Lodge year, June
30, 1978 , holdings in relati ve ly short term government securities had been inc reased to approximately $470.000 and an additional $100,000 in Treasury notes
wa:. added in July. 1978 . These purchases were funded through sales of sec urities, redemptions, interest and dividends and employer/employee contributions. These sec uriti es afford stability. liquidity and increased yields while pos:.ible changes in the management of the Plan and its investments arc being
con~idered. These possible changes are being considered due to so me rather
substantial investment losses incurred in the sale of secu rities in the first six
months of 1978.

Again we point out the complexities of a modern pension plan a nd the responsibilities attached to the management of a plan such as ours. We extend our
thank s to the Grand Lodge st:iff fo r their valued and competent services.
We reque st that an approrriation of$ I ,000 be included in the current Grand
Lodge budget to cover operating expenses of th e Committee during th e ensuing
Grand Lodge year.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON
FILM AND CREATIVE PROJECTS
To the Most Worshipful Grand l odge. F. & A . M. of California:
A year most active in the interests of California Masonry has been successfull y
concluded by this Committee and is herein reported.
Project I: As reported last year. Project I was to institu te and host a Jurisdic tional-wide annual award program to honor a Mason of outstanding character
and extraordinary achievement reflecting the infl ue nce of Masonic ideals. This
event, called the " Mason of the Year Award," was held May 25, 1978, in the
main ballroom of the Bonaventure Hotel in Los Angeles before a sell-out crowd .
Rabbi Edgar F. Magnin, former Grand Chaplain. member of West Gate Lodge
No. 335, a 50-year Mason, and long one of the nation's outstanding spi ritua l
leaders. was honored with the award .
Coordinators were Brothers Victor T. Carbone, Sydney Zaid, and Jerry Rosen. The beautiful trophy presented to Brother Magnin was designed by Thomas
J. McKimson and rendered by non-committeeman Brother Albert G . Cowan of
North Hollywood Lodge No. 542.
Jac k Rourke. Emmy award-winning te levis ion rersonality. acted as Master
of Ceremonies for a program that included Victor Carter. Ray Bolger, Chill
Wills , Pat O'Brien. Edmond A. Haddad and Brother Edwin E. "Buzz" Aldrin.
Jr.
Project II : The " Hiram Award Program" was expanded under th e leadership
of the Comm ittee. Some forty Lodges have he ld or are p lanning Hiram A ward
events at this v. riling with many other Lodges considering participation in the
program during the ensuing Masonic year.
The "Hiram Award Program" is simply the official recognition of a Brother
by his own Lodge for his devoted services to that Lodge and to Masonic prin ciples in general. It is inte nded for the Brother who. year after year. displays
his devotion without receiv ing spec ial recogn ition or special honor.
Every Lodge has many such members. You will find them at labor in th e
kitc hens. the coaching rooms. the comm ittees. anywhere that a true and steady
hand of assistance is needed . They are the living cement that binds our Fraternity
into a true Brotherhood.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F . & A. M . of California:
Your Committee on Masonic History was engaged in 1hc following aclivities
during 1he pasl year:
1. Two letters were sent to the Masters of lhe Lodges suggesting thal 1hey
write their respective Lodges· histories for the past year. To assist them,
an "Instant History .. form was included with each letter. This form provided a document which contained part of the words necessary to prepare
a Lodge's yearly history. The Lodges need only fill in that infonnation
which pertains to the individual Lodge. Jn addition, the Lodges were encouraged to send pictures of their respective Temples to the Masonic History Committee for inclusion in the Grand Lodge Archives.
2. The Committee answered many questions asked of it by the Lodges and
Brethren during the past year.
3. The Committee had pictures taken of the interior of the former Grand
Lodge Temple (as well as the home of numerous Masonic Lodges and
assoc iated bodies) at 25 Van Ness Avenue , San Francisco. The Committee
took pictures of the ou1side of the original Temple of Benic ia Lodge No.

history.

protection of Lodge assets and memorabilia (to be submitted to the
California Freemason).
e. Interviewed the Deputy Grand Master, Do nald G. lngalb, on his very
interesting life - one of considerable accomplishment.
f. Printed a three page brochure on the highlights of the history of San
Diego Lodge No . 35; the oldest Lodge in Southern California, and
gave a copy to each Brother who visited the Committee's table at this
year's Grand Lodge Communication. Also, prepared a display of San
Diego Lodge No. 35's history in pictures at the table .
5 . The Committee is engaged in a continuing project on the Masons in the
oil fields around Bakersfield in the early days.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE ON
RECOGNITION OF FOREIGN GRAND LODGES
To the Most Worihipful Grand Lodge, F . & A . M. of California:
Among the matters of Masonic import whic h have come before your Committee, we would like to comment on the following :

I

Brazil
We have received a request for recognition from the Grand Lodge of the State
of Espirito Santo, founded November 8, 1970, and attached thereto a Declaration
of Principles which we find to be regu lar in every respect. However, we are
awaiting a reply to our request for certain additional details concerning this
Grand Lodge, and we recommend that their reque st be held over until our next
Communication . Incidentally , Espirito Santo is on the Brazilian seaboard just
to the north of Rio de Janeiro, and its capital city is Victoria.
We have had no answer to our inquiries for infonnation concerning the Grand
Lodge of Acre so we recommend that this request for recognition be put over
to the next Communication. The improvement in relations between the Grand
Orient and the State Grand Lodges , which appeared to be occuring last year has
not eventuated, judging by an official bulletin from the Grand Lodge of Rio
Grande do Sul to the effect that no Treaties of amity exist between the Grand
Lodge ofGuanbara or indeed any other State Grand Lodges and the Grand Orient
of Brazil.

ItaJy
The Grand Orient of Italy is faced with a seriously disruptive situation caused
by various un-Masonic and irregular actions attributed to Grand Master Salvini.
The charges, countercharges and press publicity have created wide-spread conce rn in the Masonic world and withdrawal of recognition has been recommended
by the Commission on Information for Recognition of the Conference of Grand
Masters. It is hoped that the threat of this drastic step will have a salutary effect
on the Officers of the Grand Orient and that all necessary measures will be taken
to heal thi s serious and divisive situation. We recommend that Grand Lodge take
no action this year, in the expectation that the Grand Orient, under the new
leadership elected this October, will solve its problems. Supponing this recommendation is the fact that there are eight Lodges whose members are drawn
from the United States armed services operating under the Grand Orient of Italy,
but who have close ties to the Grand Lodge of California and who look to us
for their ritu al a nd written material. These Lodges would be put in a precarious
position without our suppon.

v
Sun Grand Lodge of Lebanon
What should not and cannot be approved are the untoward actions of Mr.
Mardi ros Boyadjian, who calls himself Grand Master of the Sun Grand Lodge
of Lebanon, to establish a Constituent all Armeni an Lodge in Los Angeles. Thi s
so called Grand Lodge is not recognized by any American Jurisdicti on , and we
consider it to be irregular and clandestine. Mr. Boyadjian has been directl y informed by our Grand Master that his actions are in violation of Masonic law and
in defiance of the well known position of Grand Lodge as to terr ito rial
sovereignty.
Most Worshipful, I move the adoption of this report and its suggestions and
recommendations.
Respectfully s ubmitted.

III

Southern Africa
The Grand Lodge of Southern Africa, with which we have long had fraternal
relations, announced that it has accepted into its membership the Brethren of
two Lodges which had been operating under a charter from the Prince Hall Grand
Lodge of Pennsylvania. The ceremonies included the consecration of both
Lodges under new names and the initiation, passing and raising of the Prince
Hall members. We suggest that this is a praiseworthy step by the Grand_ Lodge
of Southern Africa and that it should have the approval of Grand Lodge.

To the Most Worshipjiil Grand lodge . F. & A. M . of California:
No Lodges were carried over under dispensation fro m the 1977 Communication . Since then . two Lodges have been instituted and bo th have petitioned
for c harters.
Subl ime Lodge U. D. received its dispensation on Dece mber I. 1977, and
was in~tituted on January 27. 1978 . with thirty c harter members. While this
Lodge is open to all qualified applicants_ regardless of nationality . it was primarily formed to serve members o f Philippine ancestry . Twenty-one of it~ thirt y
charter members ho ld membership in the Phil ippi nes and most have continued
a~ tlual members. While the Lodge meets in Daly C ity. it draws membership

from over a considerable area with some members as far away as Vallejo and
Stockton, and with the Worshipful Master residing in Placerville about 150 mil es
away. With this small and scattered membership we must admit now that there
were some misgivings when we recommended that a dispensation be granted.
We are pleased to report that our faith in these Brethren has been justified. The
Master has never missed a meeting and the attendance of both Officers and
members has bee n far above average. They have had an increase of membership
close to 40% and have increased their net worth by about 50%.
While they still have problems to solve, we believe that their dedication to
Masonry will overcome these problem5 and that this Lodge will be a credit to
Masonry in California. We therefore reco mmend that a charter be granted.
Saddleback Valley Lodge U. D. received its dispensation on December 12,
1977, and was instituted on December 17, 1977, with 50 charter members. This
Lodge meets in Laguna Hills in southern Orange County. one of the fastest
growing and most prosperous areas of our State.
If all of their applicants become members , they will show over 40% gain in
membership this year and will have increased their net worth by about 50%.
As in most new planned communities, a sutiable meeting place has been , and
continues to be. their greatest problem. They at present meet in a community
building furnish ed fre e by Lincoln Savings, but the space and facilities are limited and will seriously hamper the future growth of the Lodge.
We have explored a number of possibilities with them for more adequate quarters and we believe that as a cbartered Lodge they will be better able to solve
this problem. We therefore recommend that their petition for a charter be
granted.
Most Worshipful Grand Master, I move that charters be granted and numbers
assigned to Sublime Lodge U. D. in the city of Daly City and Saddleback Valley
Lodge U .D. in Laguna Hills.
That portion of the Grand Secretary ' s Report dealing with charter changes has
been assigned to the Committee on Charters. The following have changed their
meeting places:

We find that all the requirements of the law have been complied with and_ I
therefore move that the Grand Secretary be autho rized to properly endorse therr
charters .
At a meeting with the Grand Master in January of this year he shared our
concern with the number of Lodges consolidating and also our concern that this
was not always the answer to the problems of the consolidating Lodges. He
therefore authorized the Committee on Charters to take an earlier look. when
invited, at Lodges contemplating consolidations. We have done so on several
occasions and believe the results have been beneficial.
In those cases where consolidations seemed the best answer , the representative
of our Committee has been able to act as a neutral third party in solving problems
and we have also been able to spot potential problems and offer constructive
advice.
There are other cases where problems of the Lodges are internal and consolidation will at best only temporarily postpone their difficulties. For such Lodges
we have worked out a format for holding " Lodge Improvement Workshops' '
designed to uncover the basic problems and to secure participation by the membership in attacking and solving these problems.
. . .
With the approval of the Grand Master we have invited the part1c1~at1on of
the Lodge Resources Development Committee and have conducted a pilot program with one of the Lodges. We are encouraged to believe that such "Lo?ge
Improvement Workshops" might mark a turning point for many marginal
Lodges. Either con;irnittee stands ready to assist when requested to do so.
Most Worshipful , this concludes the repo rt of the Committee on Charters.
Respectfully submitted.

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON TEMPLE PROPERTIES
To the Most Worshipjit! Grand Lodge, F. & A. M . of California:
Your Committee on Temple Properties is pleased to sub mit its annual report
for the 1977-1978 Grand Lodge Year. Although the Committee has been busy,
activity is down from th e last several years . The impact of the ever-increasing
costs of fuel. maintenance, taxes. insurance and building costs, together with
the proliferation of new zoning ordinances limiting the uses of land . and the
creation of even more exacting building and safety codes. are all serving to place
greater burdens on the operation of our Temples. and have te nded to d iscourage
plans for the development of new Temples.
Review of ann ua l profit and loss statements from Lodges and Temple Associations reveal that. while most are we ll managed and financially sound. many
have not adjusted income to meet the increased cost of operat ing their Temple s
and as a result may be operating at a loss, eroding thei r rese rves. Wh ile it appears
that some ta x relief may be on the horizon as a result of the recent passage uf
Proposition 13, this will not offer anything more than partial relief to the operating s t ateme nt ~ of many Temples.
Before transferring ownership uf any Temple property. Lodges or Associations should seek compete nt advice as to any property tax consequcrn.:cs under
Proposition 13.
T his Committee again recommends th at the best solu tion to stabilizing these
de fic:it operations is to set reali).tic rent sc hedules which will produce the needed
income. and at the ~ame time. establish reserves for depreciation to insure that
future repairs. remodell ing or replacement of Masonic Temples can be undertake n when requireu .
The deterioration of neighborhoods occurring in the larger urban 1.:enters plays
its pa rt both in ded ining memberships a nd attendanc e fo r Lodge s whic h have,
or use. Temples located in such areas. Residential sections wh ich forme rly supported o lder Temples now s uffer fro m the competition o f modern housing in
more desi rable ~ubur ban locales thus resulting in the shift ing o f population centers . These fo rces often work to cause Lodges either to move th eir meeting place.
or to consider consoliu at ion with another Lodge and so metimes both.
In e ither even t , whih: one Temple benetits from the increased membership
and attendance. and. often increased revenue brought about by the c hange, the
other Temple suffers the loss of those same advantages and must then search out

REPORT OF COMMITTEE ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge. F. & A. M . of California:
During this past year, your Committee on Public Schools has continued many
of the programs that have been effective and has implemented several new concepts. The hard working Committee consisted of thirty members and one
consultant.
We had t~e enthusiastic support and encouragement of our Grand Master,
M.ost Worshipful Donald B . McCaw and the Grand Lodge Elective Officers.
with whom your Chairman met on numerous occasions throughout the year. To
them and the Grand Secretary's office, particularly Marion Thomas in the Supply
Room, we express our thanks for the outstanding cooperation extendetl to our
Committee. Our Liaison Officer. has been Right Worshipful H. Douglas Lemons
who has a deep and profound interest in our Public Schools. His co unsel and
guidance thi s past year have been greatly appreciated.
The concept of having six Divisio n Coordinators a nd several Committeem en
working ':ith each Division Coordinator worked weJI and covered, geographically , Cal1fo.m1a and Hawaii to assure that every Lodge be personally co ntacted
by a Committeem an to offer assistance. The Committeem en are establishing a
folder on each and every Lodge in our Jurisdiction to perpetuate our Committee's
underst.anding of each Lodge's Public Schools programs. To better accomplish
the duties of this Committee, it is unanimously recommende d that the number
of Committeem en be increased to forty by resolution at the 1979 Grand Lodge
Communicat ion.

GENERAL PROMOTION AND PUBLICITY

Your Committee printed 15 ,000 posters , 30,000 small table tent posters,
200,000 pamphlets, several thousand appreciation certificates and 8,000 metal
buttons stating PUBLIC SCHOOLS- 1978-BUIL DING TOMOROOW TODAY. Samples were distributed to Senior Wardens at the Public Schools booth
during Grand Lodge week. Order forms were enclosed in the sample packets.
Another order form and return envelope were sent to the Lodge Secretaries in
January. The response from the Lodges was gratifying in that they almost co mpletely bought out the supply of materials noted above. No charge was made for
the pamphlets. Seyeral school districts gave a pamphlet to every st udent to take
home.
In Decem her your Committee mailed four articles about Public Schools to the
incoming Masters with the suggestion that the articles be included in the Lodges'
January . February , March and April bulletins . In April we mailed another article
for the May Lodge bulletin urging the membership to continue their support and
concern for our Public Schools throughout the year and not just in April. These
articles were well received and used by most of the Lodges in their bulletins or
paraphrased by the Master in his message for those particular months.
Public Schools Observance copy for broadcasting was delivered to the 500
radio stations in California and Hawaii by the Committeem en along with a letter
from the Grand Master urging the rad io stations to read the copy during April
as spot announcemen ts. Also, slides and copy were hand delivered to the almost
JOO television stations in o ur Jurisdic tion for airing and viewing during April.
In general, the cooperation of the stations was gratifying in the rural areas but
still left much to he desired in the larger cities. It is hoped that in the future we
can have one Committeem an work on Radio and TV publicity all year long in
hopes of penetrating the metropolitan areas for coverage and exposure .
Many local essay contests, poster contests, spelling bees, etc., were held
througho ut our Jurisdiction on a Lodge, Distric t and area basis with excellent
participation and enthusiasm. Your Committee has found that where the children
are deeply involved in any School/Lodg e observance, the participation and attendance of the public and also our Brethren and their families is excellent.

Over 50% of the Lodges reported having seen this publicity in their local news

Questionnaires were sent to all Masters in May seeking their opinions and
Lodge participation in Public Schools Observances. Many constructive thoughts
were expressed. Many local newspaper and radio features were employed by the
Lodges and Districts. Outstanding types of observances were held locally but
arc too numerous to list in this report. Almost all types of observances are noted
in the Public Schools Guidelines (green) in the Lodge Manual and it is urged
that all Masters and Wardens read these Guidelines.
In some areas Public Schools slogans were flashed on message boards. such
as the San Francisrn Giants, Los Angeles Dodgers, California Angels and at
Golden Gate Fields where the message board is generally read by passing motorists on Interstate 80 . Also the Bay Area Rapid Transit district flashed Public
Schools slogans on their BART station message boards almost 2,000,000 times
during the month of April .
In March o ur Grand Master wrote to the leadership of concordant organizations in California and Hawaii soliciting their support for the April Public
Schools Observances. The Parent Teachers Association and United Americans
for Public Schools both published the Grand Master's Proclamation and reproduced the 1978 Public Schools Poster.

MEETING WITH STATE OFFlCIALS
Your Grand Master and Chairman of your Public Schools Committee journeyed to Sacramento and spent several hours with Dr. Wilson Riles. Superintendent of Public Instruction for ~he State of California. The meeting was most
productive and in the spirit of cooperation. Dr. Riles was particularly appreciati ve and cognizant of the fact that the Masons support Public Education but ask
nothing in return from Dr. Riles· office or any governmental agency. Dr. Riles
issued a letter in January . 1978 to all School District Superintendents and County
School Superintendents advising them that the local Masonic Lodges would be
in contact with them regarding their mutual participation in some function in
April. Your Committee made copies of Dr. Riles· letter and mailed them to all
Masters. It is felt that this annual meeting with the Superintendent of Public
Instruction should be continued. Dr. Riles also issued a news release to all forms
of the media on the first of April announcing PUBLIC SCHOOLS MONTH.
In Hawaii. the local Public Schools Committee met with the Governor and
Superintendent of Education and had outstanding TV and newspaper coverage
of the State of Hawaii's full support of Public Schools Observances.

MASONRY'S INVOLVEMENT IN VOLUNTEER AND DOVES PROGRAMS
The Public Schools Committee and Grand Lodge of California cooperated
with the Los Angeles School Department in the establishment and continuation
of the DOVES (Dedicated Older Volunteers in Educational Service) program
which expanded greatly during the year. The Los Angeles City Board of Education presented the Grand Lodge of California with a plaque in recognit ion of
our efforts in this regard. The staff in the volunteer and DO YES departments
of the Los Angeles Schools has prepared a pamphlet and a 23 page guide on
how to implement a volunteer and/or DOVES type program into a school system. It is anticipated that prior to the 1979 Grand Lodge Communication , your
Committee on Public Schools will have assisted in instituting several volu nteer
programs into school districts throughout the State .
NEXT YEAR'S P UBLIC SCHOOLS OBSERVANCE-APRIL 1979
In June the Deputy Grand Master wrote to the Senior Warden of each Lodge
announcing that " PUBLIC SCHOOLS-ASSIGNMENT WITH DESTINY "
has been selected as the theme for the 1979 April Public Schools Week Observances. In September . 1978 your Committee Chairman wrote to each Senior
Warden encouraging him to stop by the Public Schools Booth at Grand Lodge
and di scuss plans for next year and pick up his sample packet. The packets
contained a 1979.metal badge and the Senior Wardens were encouraged to wear
these badges during Grand Lodge Week . The acceptance of these badges is fantastic among the Lodges and also the teachers. One School District with over
600 teachers wants a badge for each teacher to wear during April. The local
Lodge is seeing that this is accomplished . All Grand Lodge Officers will have
these badges to wear at all Public Schools Cornerstone ceremonies throughout
the coming year and at all Grand Lodge/G rand Master functions during the
month of April. With the approval of the Grand Master and Grand Lecturer, all
Public Schools Committee mailings to Masters. Wardens and Lodges are also
mailed to the Grand Lodge Officers and Inspectors in that they may be full y
aware of the tools and materials that the Lodges have at their disposal to continue
and expand our Masonic commitment in the areas of our Public Schools.
GENERAL COMMENTS
Concern was expressed this past year that we as Masons and also as individual s do not and cannot condone some of the things that are being done in our
local schools, and that we must be careful not to let the general public be of the
opinion that we support all the actions and programs of o ur school districts .
What we do support is the concept of PUBLIC EDUCATION and not the specific programs of a particular school district, with the exception of our cooperation in the volunteer and DOVES programs . The 1979 posters and other

REPORT OF
COMMITTEE ON TRAVEL ALLOWANCES

E. LLOYD HANSON , Chairman

To the Most Worshipjld Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Committee on Travel Allowances submits the following report covering
the I 29th Annual Communication of Grand Lodge.
Those entitled to Travel Allowance are the Master. or in his absence, the
ranking Warden , or in the absence of the Master and Wardens, the duly Elected
Representative in accordance with Section 1148, California Masonic Code. Past
Grand Masters, not on Committees , will be reimbursed as provided in Section
1150. California Masonic Code. When a Master or Warden from the same Lodge
is present at an Annual Communication , and one of said Officers serves on a
Grand Lodge Committee entitled to travel and expense reimbursements , he shall
be reimbursed accordingly: the other Officer shall receive reimbursement under
Section 1I48a. California Masonic Code. as the Officer representing his Lodge
on the floor of Grand Lodge.
Mileage from the various points within the State of California to San Francisco
has been taken from the published records of the California State Automobile
Association. Mileage from points in the State of Hawaii to San Francisco has
been taken from the published reports of air lines in accordance with Section
1148, California Masonic Code , Supplement. No compensation is allowed to
members from San Francisco or the immediate vicinity. Compensation of members from the State of California has been computed on the basis of eleven ( 11)
cents per mile, the rate fixed by the Committee on Finance. Co.mpensation of
members from the State of Hawaii has been figured on the basis of the published
class of fare next below first class round trip air rate of regularly scheduled major
air lines. from Honolulu to San Francisco plus inter-island air fare to Honolulu,
when necessary.
The payroll has been checked with the registration records as submitted to us
by the Committee o n Credentials, and the amounts required to meet the Travel
Allowances costs for the 1978 Annual Communication are as follows:
Past Grand Masters (not on Committees) ......... . None
Representatives of Lodg es _. .. . _ .... . .. .. . ... $37 ,466. 98
Total ... . ... . . . . .. . . . . .. . . ....... . . . . . . . . $37 ,466. 98
Checks will be ready for dis!ribution at the Registration Desk on Thursday
morning immediately following the election of the Junior Grand Warden. Bre th ren, if you are the Master or Warden representing your Lodge, or the duly
Elected Representative of your Lodge, the Committee on Travel Allowances
urgently requests you to promptly pick up your c hec k. You must present a properly stamped credential.
Arrangements have been made so that those who may wish to cash their
checks can do so at the Faim1ont Hotel Branch of the United California Bank.
Your Grand Lodge C reden tial s will serve as s uitable ide ntification .
We wish to express our sincere appreciation to members of the Grand Lodge
Office Staff for th eir cooperation shown throughout the year in assembling, preparing and computing the detail necessary for the functioning of this Committee.

REPORT OF TAXATION COMMITTEE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A . M . of California:
The purpose of your Taxation Committee is to counsel and advise the Grand
Master. the Grand Lodge , and its Constitutcnt Lodges on all general tax matters.
The Committee has no authorization to determine compliance with the tax laws.
The responsibility for tax matters rests with the Elected and Appointed Officers
and Trustees.
Generally our Masonic o rganizatio ns have received tax exempt statu s from
the Internal Reve nue Service and th e California Franchise Tax Board. Both
agencies recently have indicated more attention will be given to compliance with
the laws requiring reports from tax exempt organizations. In addition District
Direc tor of the San Francisco IRS District announced that they will be increasing
the number uf examinations of exempt organizations.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

275

All Lodges having annual gross receipts in excess of $10,000 must file I.R .S.
Form 990 "Return of Organization Exempt from Income Tax."
All Lodges. regardless of gross receipts, must file California Franc hise Tax
Board Form 199 or 1998 '· Exempt Organization Annual Information Return ."
Where wages are paid to a Lodge employee subject to Federal withholding
tax and Social Security tax the Lodge must file l.R.S. Form 941 ' ·Employe r's
Quarterly Federal Tax Return." Annually the Looge may be required tu file
I.R.S . form 940 · ·unemploy ment Tax Return." The wages paid to a Lodge
employee may be subject to California Income tax withholding , State Disability
and Unemployment Insurance and the Lodge must file Fo nn DE 3, a quarterly
return.
Service Bureaus must file similar returns.
Temple Associations must file returns with the Internal Revenue Service and
the Franchise Tax Board . The returns used are determined by the ownership and
exemption of the Temple.
Your Committee makes use of their annual report to give general circulation
to tax matters that arise during the year. We have two such subjects to bring
before you in this report .
Many Temples are exempt from taxes under Internal Revenue Code Section

501 (c)(2). These are corporations organized exclusively to hold title to property,
collecting income therefro m, and turning over the entire amount thereof, less
expense, to an organization which itself is exempt from tax. It is important to
recognize that a Temple so exempt cannot accumulate income and retain its
exemption . It must tum over the entire amo unt of such income , less expenses,
to an organization exempt from tax. There have been cases where the Internal
Revenue Service )las found the income not turned over and has assessed a large
an10unt of tax on the retained income. There have been incidents where the
Internal Revenue Service has permitted the accumulation of income for a specific
purpose. This permission should be conveyed to the corporation by a Determination Letter from the l.R.S .
The second subject has to do with sales tax . Masonic Lodges are subject to
sales tax if they make retail sales. Receipts at a rummage sale or th e like would
be subject to sales tax; there is no exception. The tax app lies to the furnishing
of meals, food, and drink unless furnished: ( 1) exclusively to members and also.
(2) less frequently than once a week. Both of these requirements must be met.
If the organization furnishes meals, food , or drink to non-members all receipts
from the furnishi ng of meals, food, or drink are subject to tax whether furnished
to members or non-members, including recei pts on occasions when furnished
exclusively to members. Meals, food, or drink paid for by members are considered fu rni shed to members even though consumed by guests who are no t
members .
There are times when the receipt is termed a donation to avoid sales tax. The
donation should be totally voluntary and no restricti on whatsoever should be
placed on the e ntrance of persons not making a donation. A set amount for the
donation , a turnstile or other restrictive device that must be passed through , or
an attendant requesting the donation at the door will be ev idence that the charge
is not voluntary.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

276

Each year we conclude our report with a reminder that tax exemption under
the law is a privilege . To maintain that privilege we must comply with the law.
As good citizens we must comply with all tax laws.
Respectfully submitted,
W. STANLEY DAVIS, Chairman

REPORT OF SPECIA L COMMI TTEE ON
MASONIC WIDOWS PROGR AM
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M . of California:
"That Masonry may be of greater service to its members and their ladies!"
So was stated the purpose of the Widows Program when its ideals were
formulated.
The ever expanding lines of communication emanating from the Grand Master's podium through the Lodge Committees to the home of the departed
Brother's wife have reached into hitherto untouched areas. Regular terminals
monitored by Lodge Chairmen have received a continuous flow of informative
messages dedicated to the betterment of this display of Masonry in action.
Thanks to the untiring efforts of the members of the Grand Lodge Committee,
and the assistance of the Area Coordinators, the necessary guidance and instruction have made it possible for seventy-five percent of the Lodges in some areas,
to ninety-five percent in others, to take part in this voluntary Grand Lodge
activity.
From the most northerly boundary to the southern extremity of the Jurisdiction
reports are being recorded of an ever increasing number of activities in which
the widows of our Brothers are participating. Work projects from numerous
Lodges are now taking groups of Brothers to the homes of these ladies to assist
them in miscellaneous repair tasks around the house.
On behalf of the Masonic Widows Committee I wish to express our sincere
gratitude for your having given us the opportunity to have been of service to our
Fraternity during this past year.
Respectfully submitted,

REPORT OF COMMI TTEE ON INSURANCE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
The Committee on Insurance keeps in close touch with our insurance brokers
and counsellors to review the insurance coverage for Grand Lodge and its Constituent Lodges.
Grand Lodge Officers frequently receive complaints from Lodges concerning
increasing expenses for conducting their basic functions, including the cost of
insurance.
At present the premium for public liability, fidelity bond and crime coverages,
All Risk insurance on personal property and paraphenalia for each Lodge is included under a master plan with a composite premium charged to each Lodge
in the per capita assessment.
The premium for Workers' Compensation insurance is charged separately to
each Lodge based on its own payroll at the governing rates.
A request was made for the Insurance Committee to investigate the possibility
of reducing the premium cost by providing a deductible of $1,000 to apply on
each loss, including Workers' Compensation.
After a carefu~ study the Committee determined that a deductible of $1,000
could not be obtained for Workers' Compensation insurance and the reduction
in premium on the other coverages was infinitesimal.
At Grand Master Donald B. McCaw's request a further analysis was made
of the results of the questionnaire submitted by the various Temple Associations
last year for data relative to insurance covering their Temple building.
This survey disclosed a large number of Temple Associations to be dangerously underinsured and the Grand Master requested the Committee to submit a
recommendation as to the type of insurance to be carried on building and contents as a minimum.
The basic coverage on the buildings should be for fire, extended coverage and
vandalism and malicious mischief on a replacement cost basis with $100 deductible applying on each claim. A higher deductible might be considered for
negotiating a rate reduction.
Coverage should include insurance which is available by endorsement to the
policy to cover the increased cost of repair due to operation of building laws and
codes and also to include extra expense required in event of demolition required
by law or for loss due to contingent liability.
Rental income should be insured for at least 50% of annual rents.
In addition to insurance covering physical damage to property , it is important,
of course, for each Temple Association to be insured for their legal liability for
bodily injury or property damage for at least a limit of $1 million per occurrence .
