COMMITTEE ON COMMERCIALISM
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F . & A. M . of California:
The Committee on Commercialism submits he rewith its report for the Masonic
Year 1978.
_During the past year there has been o nly one reported incident of a Brother
using the ' ' Square & Compass'" in an unauthorized manner . This Brother had
printe~ so me 30,000 single page advertising solicitation fiyers. Printed quite inconsptc uously _under his _signature was the "Square & Compass.·' Upon notificatio n that this was an improper use, he agreed in writing to cease using the
Symbol.
The proprietor of a " thrift store" in Oakland and Berkeley used the e mblem
on his business c ard, store front and tru ck. On first contact, he refu sed to remove
the Symbol. stating that to do so would put him out of business . This Committee
met with Grand Lodge Officers and agreed that if necessary, a ppropria te legal
proceedings wo uld be taken if this unautho ri zed use was not discontinued .
On May I, 1978 the Committee wrote the proprie tor a letter advising him that
his use o f the Sy mbol was a misdea menor under the Cali fo rnia Corporat ions
Code as well as the Penal Code.
On June I , 1978, a member of the Commerc ialism Committee revi sted the
establishments and reported that use of the Symbo l had c eased.
It is the opinion o f thi s Co mmittee th at acquiescence in the un autho rized use
of any of our Symbols could jeopardize Grand Lodge ' s exclusive use o f the
Symbo ls. Any Brothe r who should observe the unauthorized use of any Symbol
will ass ure Grand Lodge's exclusive use of the Symbols by advising his Inspec tor, or this Committee immediate ly .

. This Committee embarked upon a review of all Shrine Game reports with a
view toward standardizing th e reports. O n April 1st o f this year , the Americ an
lnsriwte of Certified Public Accountants issued an e xposure draft on reporting
practices for non -profit orga nizations . Because it would be pre matu re to for-

COLLATERAL COMM ERCIAL V ENT U RES

Since the adoption of the revised Co mmerciali sm regulati ons, the question of
what financial ventures Lodge s can engage in has reoccurred. C. M.C. 2070 prohibits Lodges from any collateral financial unde rtaking. In current vogue are
" art sales' ' by Lodges . The thrust of the plan is for an art dealer to aucti on off
art wo rk , guaranteeing the Lodge a ge ne rous min imum return . On its part. the
Lodge guarantee s a minimum attend ance at the auction. The Lodge must solicit
th e membership from the Lodge Roste r. This type of an event is contrary to the
Commercialism Regulatio ns on two counts: first , the Lodge is using the Roster
for a non-Maso nic purpose: a nd , secondly , the Lodge is ac tin g as nothing more
than a " retail outlet" for a commercial venture. In any event , where a charge
is made , the M aster and Wardens must consider the purpose of the charge. If
the c harge is sole ly to defray the cost of the e ve nt, and the e vent is solely to
further Masonic brotherhood , the charge will be proper. On the other hand , if
a Lodge sponsors a fund-rai sing event and a charge is made, this would be improper and is prohibited.
Contrasted to the above, are the regulations governing Concordant Bodi es .
A Concordant Body is not prohibited from e ngaging in a financial venture. The
only proscription is that th e ve nture no t be fraudulent. misleading, uneth ical or
illegal.
Any group inte nding to sponsor any event where a profit potential exists
should discu ss the event with its Inspector we ll in ad vance of making any
co mmitment.
This Co mmittee e xpresses its apprec iation for the helpful cooperation of the
Grand Master, the Grand Secretary and all Grand Lodge Ofticers.
Respectfully suhmitted .

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F. & A. M. of California:
Your Grand Lodge Youth Orders Committee has be.en very active on your
behaJf this past year. The Committee was expanded to forty-four (44) members
to enable us to more effectively cover this Grand Jurisdiction.
A four point program for our Committee was established to serve the needs
of the Youth Ord~rs and our Constituent Lodges as follows:

l. To work closely with the individual Lodges, and their Youth Committees.
2. To assist in obtaining well qualified , strong adult leaders for our Youth
Groups.
3. To visit the Masoni c Youth Groups.
4. To continue existing programs, such as our Youth Seminars and the Grand
Lodge Youth Night program.

March was proclaimed Youth Activities Month by our Grand Master, and he
directed each Lodge in this Grand Jurisdiction to hold appropriate activities and/
or programs with our Youth Groups. I am gratified to report to you that many
of our Lodges responded to this Proclamation with fervency and zeal. For example, Coalinga Lodge No. 387 sponsored a dinner in honor of Coalinga-A venal
Chapter, International Order of De Molay which netted more than $150.00. This
money was then turned over to the Chapter. Approximately 130 members and
guests were in attendance at this dinner-from a Lodge with a membership of
266. Truly a great event for the Lodge as well as for the Chapter. This is just
one of many reports related to this Committee this year. It has been the Committee's experience that Lodges both large and small re.ap many benefits from
joint activities with our Youth Groups . TRY IT, YOU' LL LIKE IT!
The Committee held four meetings this past year with half the Committee
meeting in the North and half in the South. In addition, several special meetings
were held. The enthusiasm expressed at these meetings was very refreshing. I

than 120 miles o ne way. T he time and effort required of these Brothers to accomplish the goals and purposes of thi s Comm itte e ca n o nly he classified as a
lahor of love.

of Ke nneth Moffatt for chairi ng the Youth Night sub-com mittee, of Ric hard

attention to some special assignments, and of Ri chard M ec ham . Way ne Geer,
and Otto Vogel fo r their e ffo rt s o n he half of the Committee this past year.

Inve stments:
Investments in securities purchased are carried at cost and securities received by gift or bequest are carried at approximate market value on
the date received. Gains and losses are recorded when investments arc sold·
Investments are not written down to market unless a permanent impairment in
the value of such investments is considered to have occurred.
Furniture. Equipment and Improvements:
Additions and betterments to property are capitalized at cost and
are not depreciated. Expenditures which repres~nt maintenance and Tepairs
are charged to e~pens c . ni.e property accounts are relieved of cost upon
disposition.
Federal and State Income Taxes:
The Grand Lodge is exempt from federal and state income taxes.

PENSlUN PIAN:

ni.e Grand Lodge contributes to the California Masonic Retirement
Plan for the benefit of all elig~ble full-time employees. Total pension
expense for the years ended June JO, 1978 and 1977 was $11,607 and H.2, 702,
respectively. Net assets held by the Plan at December 31, 1977 were i.n excess
of vested benefits.

RECOGNlTIUN OF lNVESTHENT MARKET DECLINE:

estate investment trusts Yas approxmately ~366 , 400 below cost. The Grand
Ludge has recugnized this market value d~cline as being of a permanent
nature and the inveatments have been written down to their market value
at June 30~ 1978, resulting in a loss recognition of ~361)231.

We have examined the statemen t of assets, liabilities and fund
bala nces arising from cash transact ions of Masonic Homes of California , a
nonprofit corporat i on, including t he permanent endowmen t, property and
restricted trust funds, as of June 30, i97B and 1977, and the related
stateme n ts of revenues and expenses and changes in fund balances for t he
years then ended. our exami nation s were made in accordance with general ly
accepted auditing stan dards, and accordingly included such tests of the
accounting records and such o t her auditing procedures as we considered
necessary in t he circumstances.
As described in Note 1, the policy of Ma.sonic Homes of California
is to prepare its financial statements on the mod i fied cash basis of
accoun ting; consequently, certain revenues and related assets are recogn i zed
when received rat her than when earned, and certain expenses are recognize d
when paid rathet than when incurred. Accordingly, we are requ i red to
report that th i s policy does not present the fi nancial position a nd
results of operations in conformity with generally accepted accoun ting
principles,
In our opinion , t he f i nancia l statements referred to above present
fairly the assets, liabil i ties and f und balances arising from t he cash
tran sactions of the Masonic Homes of California at June 30, 1978 a nd 1977 ,
a n d its re venues collected and expe n ses paid and changes in f und balances
for the years then ended, on the basis of accounting described in Note 1 ,
appli ed in a manner consistent with the preced ing year,

Basis of Accounti!)g:

Accounting. Generallyt revenue and related assets are recognized when

securities received by gift o r bequest are carried at approximate

Other Assets :
Other assets consist of life insurance policie s, real estate
and mineral right• as1igned or bequeathed to the Masonic Homes, These
assets are recorded at the nominal value of $1 each for accountability,
Payments by the Masonic Homes of obligations of the assignors secured
by these assets are added t o the nominal value, vith the exception of
life insurance premiums, which are charged to expense when paid.
Property:

Additions and bettennents to property are capitalized at cost
and are no~depreciated. Expenditures which represent maintenance and
repairs are charged to •xpense. 'nle property accounts are relieved of
cos t upon disposition.
Reserves for Special Purposes:
The trustees have established various spec ial reserves to
vhich are added gifts and bequests and other amount• which generally are
used at the direction of the trustees for purposes other than direct
operating expenses . The aseets represented b y the se reserves are included
i n the as sets of the General Fund.

Federal and State Income Taxes:
The Masonic Hanes of California is a charitable organization
exempt from federal and state income taxes.

S\111HARY OF SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES:

NOTE J

Basis of Accounting:
The financial sta tement s are presented on the cash basis of
Certain revenues and related assets are recognized when
received rather than when earned, and certain expenses a re recogniied
when paid rather than when incurred.

accounting.

Land, Buildings and Equipment:
Land, buildings and equipment are carried at cost and, except

for land, are depreciated on the straight-line method over estimated
useful lives of 50 years <or Temple buildings and equipment, 20 years
for furnishings and 10 years for sound and lighting equipU£nt.
Maintenance and repairs are charged to expense when paid.

Betterments

of a major nature, which eKtend the useful lives of buildings and
equipment, are capitalized.

On sa l e o r retirement, the cost and

accumulated depreciation applicable there to are eliminated from the
accounts and the difference betwee n net book value and the proceeds
from sale or re[irerrent is included in income,
Investments:

Investments in securities purchased are carried at cost and
securitie s received by gift or beques t are carried a t approximate
market value on the date received.
federal and Statt Income Taxes :

The Temple i s a charitable organiz ation exempt from federal
and state income taxes.

TOTAL GENERAL FUND

We have examined the statement of assets, liabilities and fund balances
arising from cash trans actions of Ca l ifornia Masonic Foundation , a nonprofit
corporation, at June 30 , 1978 and 1977, and the related s tatement of revenues
and expenses (or the years then ended. Our examinations were made in accordance
with generally accepted auditing standards and acco rdingly included such tests
o f the accounting records and such other auditing procedures as we considered
necessary in the circumstances.
As desc ribed in No t e 1, Tiie California Masonic Founda tion's policy is to
prepare its (inancial statements generally on the basis o f cash receipts and
disburseme nts~ consequently, certain revenues and related asse ts are recogniied
when received rather than when earned~ and certain expenses are recognized when
paid rather than when incurred. Accordingly, we are required to report that this
policy does no t present the.' financial position and results of operations in con·

formity with generally accepted accounting principle•.
In our report dated July 28, 1977, our opinion on the 1977 financial statements was qualified as being subject to the reali~ation of the carrying value of
an investment in a real estate investment trust. As explained in Note 5, the
excess of cost over market value of this investment at June 30, 1978 has been
charged to expense in the current year, as required by generally accepted
accounting principlea. Accordingly,our present opinion on the 1977 financial
statements , as presented herein, is different from that expressed in our previous
report.

ln our opinion, the aforementioned financial statements present fairly the
assets, liabilities and fund balances arising from cash cransacciona of Callfornia
Masonic Foundation at June 30, 1978 and 1977 and re venues and expenses for the years
then ended, on the basis of accounting described in Note 1 applied in a manner consistent with the preceding year.

CORRESPONDENCE REPORT

Reviews of the Proceedings of other Grand
Lodges have appeared quarterly in the "California Freemason," copies of which have
been sent to each Grand Lodge. This program will be continued.
The "California Freemason" is issued
quarterly and each copy carries additional
reviews. Hence, they do not appear in these
Proceedings.
